topics.ch: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
topics.h: Why does curd set faster in May than in January? You can find out the way a scientist would: watch, wonder, guess, test and check!
p: Science begins with an observation, something we notice using our senses or instruments, and a question about it.
A hypothesis is a possible answer to the question that can be tested, for example 'Warmth helps milk turn into curd faster.'
We test a hypothesis with an experiment or careful observations, and we record what happens as data, often in a table.
We analyse the data to see if it supports the hypothesis. If it does not, we change the hypothesis and test again. That is not failure, it is learning.
Good scientists repeat their tests, report honestly and share their results so that others can check them.

ex.q: Think it through: Aarav says, 'Plants on our balcony grow taller than the plants inside the room because they get more sunlight.' How can he investigate this?
st: Observation: balcony plants look taller.
Hypothesis: more sunlight makes the plants grow taller.
Experiment: grow two similar pots of the same plant, one in sunlight and one in a dim corner, with the same soil and the same water.
Record the height of each plant every few days in a table.
Analyse: if the sunny plant grows taller, the data supports his hypothesis.
ex.a: He should make a testable hypothesis, run a fair experiment with two similar pots, record heights, and compare the data before concluding.

topics.rl: Doctors testing a new medicine, farmers trying a new seed variety and ISRO teams testing rocket parts all follow these same steps of investigation.

rv.summary: Science starts with an observation and a question, then a testable hypothesis. We test it with a fair experiment, record data, analyse it, and change the hypothesis if needed, repeating and sharing results honestly.

Telling a testable hypothesis from an opinion
What data is and why tests are repeated
Honest reporting and sharing of results
remember: Observation → question → hypothesis → experiment → data → analysis → conclusion
Hypothesis: a possible answer that can be tested
Data: the observations and measurements we record
traps: An opinion like 'roses are most beautiful' is not a testable hypothesis
Results that do not support a hypothesis are not failure — never hide or change them

topics.ch: Exploring the Investigative World of Science
topics.h: Two friends race paper boats but one uses a bigger sheet AND blows harder. Who has the better design? Nobody can tell, because two things changed at once!
p: A variable is anything that can change in an experiment, such as temperature, amount of water or type of soil.
The independent variable is the one thing we change on purpose. The dependent variable is what we measure to see the effect.
Controlled variables are all the other things we keep the same so that the test is fair.
In a fair test we change only one variable at a time. Then any difference in results can be linked to that one change.
A control setup is kept without the change, so we can compare the results with it.

ex.q: Think it through: Isha wants to know whether warm water makes sugar dissolve faster than cold water. What are her variables?
st: What does she change on purpose? The temperature of the water, so that is the independent variable.
What does she measure? The time the sugar takes to dissolve, so that is the dependent variable.
What must stay the same? The amount of water, the amount and type of sugar, the glass and how she stirs. These are controlled variables.
ex.a: Independent: water temperature. Dependent: time to dissolve. Controlled: amount of water, amount and type of sugar, stirring and glass.

topics.rl: When a cricket coach tests a new bat, players use the same ball and pitch so that only the bat is different. That is a fair test!

rv.summary: In a fair test we change only one variable (independent), measure its effect (dependent) and keep everything else the same (controlled variables). A control setup without the change lets us compare results.

Why only one variable is changed at a time
Choosing a fair experiment and using many samples
remember: Independent variable: the one thing we change on purpose
Dependent variable: what we measure to see the effect
Controlled variables: everything else kept the same; control setup: kept without the change
traps: Don't mix up independent (changed) and dependent (measured) variables
Don't change two things at once — the test is no longer fair

topics.ch: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
topics.h: A single spoonful of garden soil can hold many millions of tiny living things. You just cannot see them without help!
p: Microorganisms (microbes) are living things too small to see with the naked eye. We need a microscope to see most of them.
The main groups are bacteria, fungi, protozoa, algae and viruses. Many are single-celled; some fungi and algae are many-celled.
Examples: Lactobacillus is a bacterium, yeast and bread mould are fungi, Amoeba and Paramecium are protozoa, and Spirogyra is an alga.
Viruses are even smaller than bacteria. They can multiply only inside the cells of another living thing.
Microbes live almost everywhere: in soil, water, air, inside our bodies, and even in very hot springs and icy places.

ex.q: Think it through: Your mother keeps a slice of bread in a warm, damp box for a few days and a fuzzy greyish-green layer appears. Is this a living thing? Which group does it belong to?
st: The fuzzy layer appeared and grew over days, so it is growing, which living things do.
It needed warmth and moisture, like many microbes.
Fuzzy threads on bread are typical of bread mould, which is a fungus.
ex.a: Yes, it is bread mould, a living fungus. (Mouldy food should not be eaten or sniffed closely.)

topics.rl: Green slime on a pond or on the walls of a water tank is often algae, and the black spots on old, damp bread are fungi.

rv.summary: Microorganisms are living things too small to see without a microscope. The main groups are bacteria, fungi, protozoa, algae and viruses; viruses multiply only inside other living cells, and microbes live almost everywhere.

Viruses multiply only inside host cells
Recognising what is and is not a microorganism

topics.ch: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
topics.h: In 1665 Robert Hooke looked at a thin slice of cork and saw rows of tiny boxes. He called them 'cells', and biology was never the same again!
p: The cell is the basic unit of life. All living things are made of one cell (unicellular, like Amoeba) or many cells (multicellular, like us).
Robert Hooke named cells in 1665. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, using his own lenses, was the first to see living microbes.
Most cells have a cell membrane (outer boundary), cytoplasm (jelly-like filling) and a nucleus (control centre).
Plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts (where food is made using sunlight) and usually a large vacuole. Animal cells do not have a cell wall.
A light microscope magnifies using two lenses. Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification.

ex.q: Think it through: A microscope has a 10× eyepiece and a 40× objective lens. How many times bigger does a cell look?
st: Each lens magnifies in turn, so we multiply.
ex.a: 400 times bigger

topics.rl: Pathology labs use microscopes to look at blood cells when a doctor orders a blood test.

rv.summary: The cell is the basic unit of life; organisms are unicellular or multicellular. Most cells have a membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus, and plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole; Hooke named cells in 1665.
focus: Parts of a cell and their jobs
Total magnification and levels cell → tissue → organ
remember: Cell membrane (boundary), cytoplasm (jelly-like filling), nucleus (control centre)
Plant cells also have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a large vacuole; animal cells have no cell wall
Total magnification = eyepiece × objective; Robert Hooke named cells in 1665

Don't add the lens powers — multiply them (10 × 40 = 400)

topics.ch: The Invisible Living World: Beyond Our Naked Eye
topics.h: The fluffy idli on your plate, the curd in your raita and the medicine that cured your infection all owe something to microbes!
p: Lactobacillus bacteria turn milk into curd. Yeast and bacteria ferment idli and dosa batter, and the gas they make (carbon dioxide) makes batter and bread dough rise.
Rhizobium bacteria live in the root nodules of pulse plants (legumes) like gram and peas and fix nitrogen from the air, making the soil richer.
Decomposer microbes break down dead plants, animals and kitchen waste into compost (manure), returning nutrients to the soil.
Antibiotics such as penicillin are made from microbes. Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin from a mould in 1928. Antibiotics work against bacteria, not viruses.
Harmful microbes (pathogens) cause diseases: typhoid and cholera (bacteria), common cold and flu (viruses), malaria (a protozoan). Some microbes also spoil food.

ex.q: Think it through: Why do we keep cooked dal in the refrigerator overnight rather than on the kitchen shelf?
st: Microbes from the air settle on food and grow on it.
They grow and multiply fastest in warm conditions.
Cold slows their growth, so the dal stays fresh for longer.
ex.a: Low temperature slows the growth of the microbes that spoil food.

topics.rl: Pickles last for months because salt, oil and spices stop most microbes from growing. Jams use lots of sugar for the same reason.

rv.summary: Useful microbes make curd (Lactobacillus), ferment batter (yeast), fix nitrogen (Rhizobium), make compost and give antibiotics like penicillin (Fleming, 1928). Harmful microbes cause diseases such as typhoid, cholera (bacteria), cold, flu (viruses) and malaria (protozoan), and spoil food.
focus: Uses of microbes in food, farming and medicine
Diseases and the type of microbe that causes each
Antibiotics work on bacteria, not viruses
Ways to slow food spoilage: cold, salt
remember: Lactobacillus → curd; yeast → batter and dough rise (carbon dioxide); Rhizobium → nitrogen fixation in legume root nodules
Penicillin discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 from a mould
Typhoid, cholera: bacteria; cold, flu: viruses; malaria: protozoan Plasmodium (female Anopheles mosquito)
traps: Antibiotics do not cure viral illnesses like the common cold
Malaria is caused by a protozoan, not a virus or bacterium
Decomposers cannot break down most plastics

topics.h: A cough in one corner of a crowded bus can travel further than you think. How do germs hop from one person to another?
p: Good health means physical, mental and social well-being, not just the absence of disease.
Communicable (infectious) diseases are caused by pathogens such as bacteria, viruses and protozoa, and can spread from one person to another.
They spread through the air (coughs and sneezes: cold, flu, tuberculosis), through contaminated water or food (cholera, typhoid), through close contact, or through carriers called vectors.
Mosquitoes are common vectors: female Anopheles mosquitoes spread malaria, and Aedes mosquitoes spread dengue and chikungunya.
Non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and heart disease do not spread from person to person. They are linked to lifestyle, diet, age and family history.

ex.q: Think it through: Several people in one colony fall ill with loose motions and vomiting after drinking water from a leaking pipeline. What is the likely cause?
st: Many people got the same illness at about the same time.
They all shared the same water source, which was leaking.
Dirty water can carry bacteria that cause diseases like cholera.
ex.a: The water was probably contaminated with disease-causing microbes, so it is a water-borne communicable disease.

topics.rl: During the monsoon, municipal teams spray against mosquitoes and check for stagnant water because cases of dengue and malaria often rise in this season.

rv.summary: Good health means physical, mental and social well-being. Communicable diseases are caused by pathogens and spread through air, water, food, contact or vectors like mosquitoes, while non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and heart disease do not spread from person to person.
focus: How diseases spread: air, water/food, contact, vectors
remember: Air: cold, flu, tuberculosis; water/food: cholera, typhoid
Female Anopheles → malaria; Aedes → dengue and chikungunya; a carrier is a vector
Non-communicable: diabetes, heart disease — linked to lifestyle, diet, age, family history
traps: Don't mix up mosquitoes — Anopheles spreads malaria, Aedes spreads dengue
Male mosquitoes do not spread malaria; only infected females bite
Diabetes and heart disease cannot be 'caught' from others

topics.h: Washing your hands with soap for about 20 seconds is one of the cheapest and most powerful medicines in the world!
p: Wash hands with soap and water before eating, after using the toilet and after playing outdoors.
Drink clean water: boiling, filtering or purifying water kills or removes many pathogens.
Cover your mouth and nose with a tissue or your elbow when you cough or sneeze, to stop droplets spreading.
Do not let water collect in coolers, pots, tyres or flower vases, since mosquitoes breed in stagnant water. Mosquito nets and repellents help too.
A balanced diet, exercise, good sleep and staying away from tobacco keep the body strong. A lack of certain nutrients causes deficiency diseases, like scurvy from too little vitamin C.

ex.q: Think it through: Dengue cases are rising in Sana's neighbourhood. Name two things her family can do at home to stay safe.
st: Dengue is spread by Aedes mosquitoes.
Mosquitoes lay eggs in still, clean water.
So remove standing water and avoid getting bitten.
ex.a: Empty and clean coolers, pots and buckets regularly so mosquitoes cannot breed, and use mosquito nets, screens or repellents and full-sleeve clothes.

topics.rl: Schools in India encourage handwashing before the mid-day meal, which helps cut stomach infections among children.

rv.summary: We prevent diseases by washing hands with soap, drinking boiled or purified water, covering coughs, not letting water collect for mosquitoes, and covering food. A balanced diet, exercise and good sleep keep us strong; too little vitamin C causes scurvy.
focus: Deficiency diseases: vitamin C and scurvy
remember: Wash hands before eating and after the toilet; boil or purify drinking water
Empty coolers, pots and tyres so mosquitoes cannot breed; use nets and repellents
Lack of vitamin C → scurvy; amla, guava, lemon and oranges are rich in vitamin C
traps: Hands that look clean can still carry germs
Mosquito nets do not prevent diabetes — exercise and diet do
Keeping water in sunlight for a minute does not make it safe to drink

topics.h: Your body has its own security force. Vaccines are like a training drill that shows the guards a 'wanted poster' before the real thief arrives!
p: The immune system defends the body. White blood cells fight pathogens and make antibodies that attach to specific germs.
After an infection, the immune system often 'remembers' the germ, so it can fight it faster next time. This is immunity.
A vaccine contains weakened or killed germs, or harmless parts of them. It trains the immune system to make antibodies without causing the disease.
Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796. Thanks to vaccination, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980, and India was certified polio-free in 2014.
Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses. Using them without a doctor's advice or stopping them early helps bacteria become resistant (antimicrobial resistance).

ex.q: Think it through: Why does a baby get vaccines even when the baby is perfectly healthy?
st: Vaccines must act before the germ attacks.
The vaccine trains the immune system to recognise the germ.
If the real germ comes later, the body is ready to fight it quickly.
ex.a: Vaccines prevent disease, so they are given before infection, while the child is healthy.

topics.rl: India's Universal Immunisation Programme gives free vaccines to children, like BCG against tuberculosis and polio drops, at government health centres.

rv.summary: The immune system, with white blood cells and antibodies, defends the body and remembers germs (immunity). Vaccines train it safely; Jenner made the smallpox vaccine in 1796, smallpox was eradicated in 1980 and India became polio-free in 2014. Antibiotics work on bacteria, not viruses.
focus: What a vaccine contains and why it is given to healthy children
Key dates: Jenner 1796, smallpox eradicated 1980, India polio-free 2014
Correct use of antibiotics and antimicrobial resistance
remember: White blood cells fight pathogens and make antibodies
Vaccine = weakened or killed germs, or harmless parts of them
Jenner: smallpox vaccine 1796; smallpox eradicated 1980; India polio-free 2014

Don't stop an antibiotic course early — it helps bacteria become resistant

topics.h: In 1820 a teacher named Hans Christian Oersted noticed a compass needle twitch every time he switched on a current. Electricity was secretly making magnetism!
p: A wire carrying an electric current produces a magnetic field around it. This is the magnetic effect of current.
A compass needle placed near the wire deflects (turns) when the current flows and returns when the current stops.
If the direction of the current is reversed, the compass needle deflects in the opposite direction.
Winding the wire into a coil makes the magnetic effect stronger. A current-carrying coil behaves like a bar magnet with a north and a south pole.
Safety: do these activities only with dry cells and a switch, under adult supervision. Never use the electricity from wall sockets.

ex.q: Think it through: Tara places a compass under a wire connected to a cell and a switch. The needle moves when she presses the switch. What happens if she swaps the cell's connections?
st: The needle moves because the current makes a magnetic field.
Swapping the connections reverses the direction of the current.
A reversed current makes a reversed magnetic field.
ex.a: The needle will deflect in the opposite direction.

topics.rl: Every electric motor in a ceiling fan, mixer-grinder or washing machine works because current-carrying coils behave like magnets.

rv.summary: A wire carrying current produces a magnetic field around it, so a nearby compass needle deflects; reversing the current reverses the deflection (Oersted, 1820). Winding the wire into a coil makes the effect stronger, and the coil behaves like a bar magnet.
focus: Observing the magnetic effect with a compass
Why a coil is stronger, and coil as a bar magnet
remember: Oersted discovered the magnetic effect of current in 1820
Reversing the current reverses the compass deflection
A current-carrying coil acts like a bar magnet with north and south poles
traps: The needle moves only while the current flows, not because the wire is iron
Never use wall sockets for these experiments — use dry cells and a switch

topics.h: A giant crane in a scrapyard lifts a whole car with a magnet, then drops it with the flick of a switch. That is an electromagnet at work!
p: An electromagnet is a coil of insulated wire wound around a soft iron core (like an iron nail). It is a magnet only while current flows.
It becomes stronger with more turns of wire, a larger current (for example, more cells), and an iron core inside the coil.
Reversing the current reverses its north and south poles.
Unlike a permanent magnet, an electromagnet can be switched on and off, and its strength can be changed.
Uses: cranes that lift iron scrap, electric bells, loudspeakers, electric motors and machines that separate iron from waste.

ex.q: Think it through: Dev's nail electromagnet picks up 4 pins. He wants it to pick up more pins. Suggest two changes.
st: Strength depends on the number of turns of wire.
Strength also depends on the size of the current.
So add turns, or use more cells in series (with adult supervision).
ex.a: Wind more turns of wire around the nail, or increase the current by adding another cell.

topics.rl: In an electric bell, an electromagnet pulls a metal strip that makes the hammer hit the gong, again and again, very fast. Trrring!

rv.summary: An electromagnet is a coil of insulated wire around a soft iron core that is a magnet only while current flows. It gets stronger with more turns, more current and an iron core; reversing the current reverses its poles, and it can be switched on and off.
focus: Parts of an electromagnet and when it works
Uses: cranes, electric bells, loudspeakers, motors
remember: Electromagnet = insulated coil around a soft iron core; a magnet only while current flows
Stronger with more turns, larger current, iron core
Uses: scrap cranes, electric bells, loudspeakers, electric motors
traps: Fewer turns or a plastic core make it weaker, not stronger
Bare wire won't do — the coil must be insulated

topics.h: Why does an old-style bulb get too hot to touch while an LED stays cool? It is all about the heating effect of current!
p: When current flows through a wire, the wire gets heated. This is the heating effect of electric current.
The heat produced depends on the material, length and thickness of the wire and on the size of the current.
Heaters, electric irons, toasters, kettles and immersion rods use a coil of nichrome alloy, which gets very hot without melting.
In a filament bulb, a thin tungsten filament glows white-hot, but most of the energy is lost as heat. LEDs give the same light using much less electricity.
A fuse is a safety device with a wire of low melting point. If too much current flows, the wire melts and breaks the circuit. Today many homes use MCBs, which switch off automatically.

ex.q: Think it through: Too many appliances are plugged into one extension board and the fuse in the house 'blows'. Was the fuse faulty?
st: Many appliances together draw a large current.
A large current heats the fuse wire strongly.
The fuse wire melts and breaks the circuit before the house wiring overheats.
ex.a: No. The fuse worked correctly and protected the wiring from overheating and possible fire.

topics.rl: Electrical appliances in India carry the ISI or BIS mark to show they meet safety standards. Always ask an adult or an electrician to replace a fuse.

rv.summary: Current flowing through a wire heats it (heating effect). Heaters and irons use nichrome coils, filament bulbs use tungsten (but waste energy as heat, unlike LEDs), and a fuse or MCB breaks the circuit when too much current flows.

How a fuse and an MCB protect a circuit

LED versus filament bulb and safe habits

Fuse: low-melting wire that melts when current is too large; MCB switches off automatically
LEDs waste much less energy as heat than filament bulbs
traps: A blown fuse usually means it did its job, not that it was faulty
A fuse wire must have a low, not high, melting point

topics.h: A kabaddi raider pushes, a magnet pulls a pin without touching it, and a mango falls from the tree. All three are forces, but only one needs a touch!
p: A force is a push or a pull. Its SI unit is the newton (N). A force has both a size (magnitude) and a direction.
A force can start or stop motion, change speed, change direction, or change the shape of an object.
Contact forces act only when objects touch: muscular force (from our muscles), friction, and the push of a spring or a stretched rubber band.
Non-contact forces act from a distance: magnetic force, electrostatic force (a rubbed balloon pulling bits of paper) and gravitational force.
Liquids push upward on objects placed in them. This upward force is called upthrust or buoyant force; it is why a mug feels lighter under water.

ex.q: Think it through: You rub a plastic comb on dry hair and bring it near tiny bits of paper. They jump up to the comb. What kind of force is this?
st: The comb and the paper did not touch before the paper moved.
So it is a non-contact force.
Rubbing gave the comb an electric charge, so it is an electrostatic force.
ex.a: A non-contact force, the electrostatic force.

topics.rl: A goalkeeper stopping a football, a fridge magnet holding a list and a bucket of water feeling lighter inside a well are all forces in action.

rv.summary: A force is a push or pull with size and direction, measured in newtons. It can change motion, speed, direction or shape. Contact forces (muscular, friction, spring) need touching; non-contact forces (magnetic, electrostatic, gravity) act from a distance. Liquids push up (upthrust).

remember: SI unit of force: newton (N)

traps: A force does not change an object's mass or colour

topics.h: Try walking on a freshly mopped marble floor in socks. Whoosh! You slip because there is too little friction under your feet.
p: Friction is a contact force that opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact.
Rougher surfaces produce more friction. Pressing the surfaces together harder also increases friction.
Friction is useful: it lets us walk, write, hold things and stop a cycle with brakes. Treads on tyres and soles increase grip.
Friction also wears out shoes and machine parts and produces heat. Lubricants (oil, grease), polishing and ball bearings reduce it.
Rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction, which is why wheels help. Air and water also oppose motion (drag), so fast vehicles, birds and fish have streamlined shapes.

ex.q: Think it through: A heavy box of books is hard to push across the floor. How can you move it more easily?
st: Sliding friction between the box and floor resists the push.
Rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction.
So put the box on a trolley with wheels, or on rollers.
ex.a: Use wheels or rollers, so rolling friction (smaller) replaces sliding friction.

topics.rl: Rubbing your palms together on a cold Shimla morning warms them up. That warmth is the heat produced by friction.

rv.summary: Friction is a contact force opposing relative motion between surfaces; rough surfaces and harder pressing increase it. It helps us walk, write and brake, but wears parts and makes heat. Lubricants and ball bearings reduce it; rolling friction is less than sliding; streamlining cuts drag.
focus: Direction of friction and what increases it
Useful and harmful effects of friction
Ways to reduce friction: lubricants, wheels, ball bearings
remember: Friction opposes relative motion; rougher or harder-pressed surfaces give more friction
Rolling friction < sliding friction
Oil and grease are lubricants; treads increase grip
traps: Friction does not act in the direction of motion
Treads increase friction, they don't reduce it
Wet, soapy floors have less friction, not more

topics.h: An astronaut weighing 600 newtons on Earth would weigh only about 100 newtons on the Moon, yet she would still have exactly the same amount of 'stuff' in her body!
p: Gravity is the force with which the Earth pulls every object towards its centre. Every object with mass attracts others, but the Earth's pull is what we notice.
Mass is the amount of matter in an object. It is measured in kilograms (kg) and stays the same everywhere.
Weight is the force of gravity on an object. Since it is a force, it is measured in newtons (N), using a spring balance.
On Earth, weight (in N) ≈ mass (in kg) × 9.8. So a 1 kg bag of rice weighs about 9.8 N.
The Moon's gravity is about one-sixth of the Earth's, so an object weighs about one-sixth as much on the Moon, while its mass does not change.

ex.q: Think it through: A watermelon has a mass of 5 kg. What is its weight on Earth (taking 9.8 N for each kg)?
st: Weight = mass × 9.8
ex.a: About 49 N

topics.rl: When ISRO's Chandrayaan-3 lander touched down near the Moon's south pole in 2023, it weighed far less there than on Earth, though its mass was unchanged.

rv.summary: Gravity pulls objects towards the Earth's centre. Mass is the amount of matter, in kg, and never changes. Weight is gravity's pull, a force in newtons, measured with a spring balance: weight ≈ mass × 9.8 on Earth. On the Moon weight is about one-sixth, but mass stays the same.
focus: Units: kg for mass, N for weight
Weight on the Moon is about one-sixth
remember: Weight (N) ≈ mass (kg) × 9.8; a 1 kg bag weighs about 9.8 N
Mass stays the same everywhere; weight changes with gravity
Spring balance measures weight
traps: Don't divide mass by 6 on the Moon — only weight changes
Weight is in newtons, not kilograms
Gravity pulls towards the Earth's centre, not just 'downward'

topics.h: Why does a sharp knife cut a tomato easily while a blunt one squashes it? Same push, very different pressure!
p: Pressure is the force acting on a unit area: pressure = force ÷ area. Its SI unit is the pascal (Pa); 1 Pa = 1 N per square metre.
The same force on a smaller area gives more pressure. That is why knives are sharp and nails are pointed, while school bags have wide straps.
Liquids press on the bottom and sides of their containers. Liquid pressure increases with depth, so water spurts farthest from the lowest hole in a bottle.
Air also has weight and presses on everything in all directions. This is atmospheric pressure; at sea level it is about 1,01,325 Pa (roughly 1 lakh pascal).
Air pressure decreases as we go higher, which is why ears may 'pop' on a drive up to the hills or in an aeroplane.

ex.q: Think it through: A force of 200 N acts on an area of 4 square metres. What is the pressure?
st: Pressure = force ÷ area
ex.a: 50 Pa

topics.rl: Dams are built much thicker at the bottom than at the top because water pressure is greatest at the bottom.

rv.summary: Pressure = force ÷ area, measured in pascals. The same force on a smaller area gives more pressure (sharp knives, wide bag straps). Liquid pressure increases with depth. Air presses in all directions; atmospheric pressure is about 1,01,325 Pa at sea level and falls with height.
focus: Pressure = force ÷ area and the pascal
Effect of area: knives, nails, bag straps
Air pressure in all directions, decreasing with height
remember: 1 Pa = 1 N per square metre
Atmospheric pressure at sea level ≈ 1,01,325 Pa
Dams are thicker at the bottom because pressure rises with depth
traps: Smaller area means more pressure, not less
Air pressure decreases, not increases, as you go higher
The newton is the unit of force, not pressure

topics.h: On a hot afternoon at Marina Beach in Chennai, a cool breeze blows in from the sea. By night it turns around. Why does the wind change sides?
p: Wind is moving air. Air moves from a region of high pressure to a region of low pressure. The bigger the pressure difference, the faster the wind.
Warm air expands, becomes lighter and rises. Cooler air moves in to take its place. This creates wind.
Land heats up and cools down faster than water. By day, land is warmer, so a sea breeze blows from sea to land. By night, land is cooler, so a land breeze blows from land to sea.

Uneven heating on a huge scale drives the monsoon. In summer the land of India becomes very hot, and moist winds from the oceans blow in and bring the rains (the south-west monsoon, mainly June to September).
Fast-moving air has lower pressure. Strong winds over a roof can lower the pressure above it so that a weak roof may lift off.

ex.q: Think it through: You hold a strip of paper below your lips and blow over its top. The strip rises. Why?
st: Blowing makes the air above the strip move fast.
Fast-moving air has lower pressure.
The still air below has higher pressure and pushes the strip up.
ex.a: The pressure above the strip is lowered by the fast-moving air, so the higher pressure below pushes it up.

topics.rl: Farmers across India watch for the monsoon's arrival because most of the country's yearly rain falls in these months. A wind vane shows wind direction and an anemometer measures wind speed.

rv.summary: Wind is air moving from high to low pressure; warm air expands and rises while cooler air moves in. Land heats and cools faster than water, giving a sea breeze by day and a land breeze by night. Uneven heating drives the south-west monsoon (June to September). Fast-moving air has lower pressure.
focus: High to low pressure and rising warm air
remember: Day: sea breeze (sea → land); night: land breeze (land → sea)
South-west monsoon: mainly June to September
Anemometer measures wind speed; barometer measures air pressure
traps: Wind does not blow from low to high pressure
Land, not sea, cools faster at night
Fast-moving air has lower, not higher, pressure

topics.h: Weather scientists can now spot a cyclone days before it reaches the coast. Their warnings help millions of people get to safety in time!
p: Thunderstorms often form on hot, humid days when warm, moist air rises quickly, forms tall clouds and brings lightning, thunder, strong winds and heavy rain.
A cyclone forms over warm ocean water. Moist air rises, creating a region of very low pressure, and winds spiral in around it at high speed. The calm centre is called the eye.
The same kind of storm is called a hurricane near the Americas and a typhoon in the western Pacific. In India, more cyclones form in the Bay of Bengal than in the Arabian Sea.
The India Meteorological Department (IMD) tracks cyclones with satellites and radar and issues warnings. Coastal states run cyclone shelters and evacuation plans.

Cyclone safety: follow official warnings, keep an emergency kit (water, dry food, torch, first-aid, charged phone, documents), move to a shelter if told, stay indoors, keep away from fallen wires, and fishermen should not go to sea.

ex.q: Think it through: Lightning flashes and you are playing in an open ground. A tall, lonely tree stands nearby. Should you shelter under it?
st: Lightning tends to strike tall objects.
A lonely tree in an open field is the tallest object around.
Shelter in a proper building or a closed car instead; if there is none, crouch low away from trees and poles.
ex.a: No. Move into a building quickly. If you cannot, crouch low in the open, away from tall trees and poles.

topics.rl: Odisha's early warnings and cyclone shelters have helped move lakhs of people to safety before powerful cyclones, saving many lives.

rv.summary: Thunderstorms form when warm, moist air rises fast. Cyclones form over warm oceans around a calm, very low-pressure eye; they are hurricanes near the Americas and typhoons in the western Pacific. In India the Bay of Bengal has more cyclones, and the IMD issues warnings.
focus: The eye and low pressure at the centre
Names in different regions; Bay of Bengal versus Arabian Sea
IMD warnings and cyclone and lightning safety
remember: Cyclone centre (eye): calm, very low pressure
Hurricane: near the Americas; typhoon: western Pacific
IMD issues cyclone warnings; keep a torch, water, dry food, first-aid, charged phone
traps: Never shelter under a lone tall tree in lightning
A tsunami is caused by undersea earthquakes, not winds
The cyclone's centre has very low, not high, pressure

topics.t: Matter is made of tiny particles
topics.h: Light an agarbatti in one corner of the room and soon the whole room smells of it. The smell travels without anyone carrying it. How?
p: All matter is made of extremely tiny particles, far too small to see even with an ordinary microscope.
There are spaces between particles. When sugar dissolves in water, its particles fit into the spaces between water particles.
Particles are always moving. When particles of one substance spread out and mix with another by themselves, it is called diffusion.
Diffusion is faster when the temperature is higher, because heated particles move faster. Diffusion is fastest in gases and slowest in solids.
Particles attract each other. This force of attraction holds them together; it is strongest in solids and weakest in gases.

ex.q: Think it through: A drop of ink is gently added to a glass of hot water and another to a glass of cold water. In which glass does the colour spread through faster, and why?
st: The colour spreads because ink particles and water particles keep moving and mixing: diffusion.
Heat gives particles more energy, so they move faster.
Faster particles mix sooner.
ex.a: In the hot water, because its particles move faster and diffusion happens more quickly.

topics.rl: You can tell someone is frying pakoras in the kitchen from your room. The smell particles diffuse through the air, and hot food's smell spreads quickly.

rv.summary: All matter is made of extremely tiny particles with spaces between them. Particles are always moving and mix on their own by diffusion, which is faster at higher temperatures and fastest in gases. Particles attract each other, most strongly in solids and least in gases.
focus: Evidence for tiny particles and spaces between them
Diffusion and what speeds it up
Attraction between particles in different states
remember: Diffusion: fastest in gases, slowest in solids
Heating makes particles move faster, not grow bigger
Attraction between particles: strongest in solids, weakest in gases
traps: Dissolved sugar does not disappear — it fills spaces between water particles
Heat does not make particles bigger

topics.t: Solids, liquids, gases and the spaces between particles
topics.h: Why can a lot of CNG be squeezed into the small cylinder of an auto-rickshaw, but you cannot squeeze a brick even a little?
p: Solids: particles are very closely packed with very little space between them and strong attraction. They only vibrate in place, so solids have a fixed shape and a fixed volume.
Liquids: particles are a little farther apart with weaker attraction. They can slide past each other, so liquids have a fixed volume but take the shape of their container.
Gases: particles are far apart with very weak attraction and move freely in all directions. Gases have no fixed shape or volume and fill any container.
Because gas particles have large spaces between them, gases can be compressed a lot. Solids and liquids can hardly be compressed.
Changing the state of a substance (like ice to water) changes the arrangement and spacing of its particles, not the particles themselves.

ex.q: Think it through: You press the plunger of a sealed syringe filled with air, then one filled with water. What happens and why? (Do not point a syringe at anyone.)
st: Air particles have large spaces between them.
Pressing pushes air particles closer, so the plunger moves in a lot.
Water particles are already close together, so the plunger hardly moves.
ex.a: The air syringe compresses easily but the water syringe hardly at all, because gas particles have much more space between them.

topics.rl: CNG for autos and buses and oxygen for hospitals are stored in compressed form in strong cylinders, possible only because gases can be squeezed.

rv.summary: Solid particles are tightly packed and only vibrate: fixed shape and volume. Liquid particles slide past each other: fixed volume, no fixed shape. Gas particles are far apart and move freely, filling any container and compressing easily. Changing state rearranges the same particles.
focus: Particle arrangement in solids, liquids and gases
Shape and volume of each state
What changes during a change of state
remember: Solid: fixed shape and volume; liquid: fixed volume only; gas: neither
Gases compress easily because of large spaces between particles
Change of state changes arrangement and spacing, not the particles
traps: Liquids do not have a fixed shape
Solid particles still vibrate — they are not motionless
Melting does not create new kinds of particles

topics.h: Why does water in a clay matka stay cool on a hot summer day, even without a fridge?
p: Heating gives particles energy. At the melting point a solid turns into a liquid; ice melts at 0 °C.
At the boiling point a liquid turns into a gas throughout its volume. Pure water boils at 100 °C at sea level.
Evaporation is the change of a liquid into vapour from its surface, at temperatures below boiling. It is faster when it is hot, windy, dry, and when the surface area is larger.
Evaporation causes cooling: the faster-moving particles escape and take energy away. Sweating and the clay matka both cool this way.
Condensation is gas turning into liquid, as on the outside of a cold glass. Some solids, like camphor and naphthalene balls, change directly into vapour; this is sublimation.

ex.q: Think it through: Clothes dry faster on a sunny, windy day than on a humid, still day. Why?
st: Drying of clothes is evaporation of water.
Sunshine heats the water particles, so more escape.
Wind carries away the vapour, and dry air can take in more vapour than humid air.
ex.a: Heat, wind and dry air all speed up evaporation.

topics.rl: Drops forming on the outside of a cold glass of nimbu pani are not leaking; they are water vapour from the air condensing on the cold surface.

rv.summary: Solids melt at the melting point (ice: 0 °C); liquids boil throughout at the boiling point (water: 100 °C). Evaporation happens from the surface below boiling, faster when hot, windy or dry, and causes cooling. Condensation turns vapour into liquid; sublimation turns solid into vapour.
focus: Melting and boiling points of water
Evaporation versus boiling and factors affecting evaporation
remember: Ice melts at 0 °C; water boils at 100 °C at sea level
Evaporation is faster when hot, windy, dry, with a larger surface area
Camphor and naphthalene sublime: solid → vapour directly
traps: Drops on a cold glass come from the air, not through the glass
Evaporation does not need 100 °C
Humid, still air slows drying

topics.ch: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures
topics.h: Everything around you, from your pencil to the Taj Mahal, is built from just 118 known 'ingredients' called elements!
p: An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom. It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical methods.
118 elements are known today. Examples: hydrogen, oxygen, carbon, iron, copper, gold and sulfur.
Each element has a symbol of one or two letters, the first always a capital: H (hydrogen), O (oxygen), C (carbon), N (nitrogen), Fe (iron), Cu (copper), Na (sodium), Au (gold), Ag (silver).
Most elements are metals. Metals are usually shiny, can be beaten into sheets (malleable) and drawn into wires (ductile), and conduct heat and electricity well.
Non-metals such as sulfur, carbon and oxygen are usually dull and brittle when solid, and are poor conductors. (Graphite, a form of carbon, is an exception: it conducts electricity.)

ex.q: Think it through: A shiny piece of material is beaten into a thin sheet and conducts electricity in a circuit. Is it more likely a metal or a non-metal?
st: Shiny lustre is a property of metals.
Being beaten into sheets (malleability) is a property of metals.
Good electrical conduction is a property of metals.
ex.a: It is most likely a metal.

topics.rl: Copper is used for electric wires and aluminium for cooking vessels and foil because metals conduct electricity and heat well.

rv.summary: An element is a pure substance of only one kind of atom that cannot be broken down chemically; 118 are known. Each has a one- or two-letter symbol, like Fe for iron and Na for sodium. Most are metals (shiny, malleable, ductile, good conductors); non-metals like sulfur are dull and brittle.
remember: 118 elements are known
Fe = iron (ferrum), Na = sodium (natrium), Cu = copper, Au = gold, Ag = silver
Malleable: beaten into sheets; ductile: drawn into wires
traps: Na is sodium, not nitrogen (N)
Water is a compound and air is a mixture, not elements
Graphite is a non-metal that does conduct electricity

topics.ch: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures
topics.h: Hydrogen is a gas that burns. Oxygen helps things burn. Join them chemically and you get water, which puts out fires! How can that be?
p: A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more elements combine chemically in a fixed proportion.
A compound has properties different from the elements it is made of. Sodium (a very reactive metal) and chlorine (a poisonous gas) form common salt, which we eat.
Every compound has a fixed composition and a formula: water is H₂O (2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom), carbon dioxide is CO₂, common salt is NaCl.
A compound can be split into its elements only by chemical methods, not by simple physical methods like filtering or using a magnet.
Energy (like heat or light) is often taken in or given out when a compound is formed.

ex.q: Think it through: Iron filings and sulfur powder are mixed. A magnet pulls out the iron. After the mixture is strongly heated in a lab, the new black solid is no longer attracted by the magnet. What happened?
st: Before heating, iron kept its own property of being attracted to a magnet: it was a mixture.
Heating made iron and sulfur combine chemically.
The new substance, iron sulfide, has new properties, so the magnet cannot pull out the iron.
ex.a: A compound (iron sulfide) was formed, with properties different from iron and sulfur. (This is a lab demonstration only.)

topics.rl: The sugar in your kheer is a compound of carbon, hydrogen and oxygen, yet it looks and tastes nothing like charcoal or any gas!

rv.summary: A compound is two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion, with properties different from its elements (sodium + chlorine → edible salt). It has a formula, like H₂O, CO₂ or NaCl, and can be split only by chemical methods. Energy is often taken in or given out when it forms.
focus: Definition of a compound and fixed proportion
Separating compounds only by chemical methods
remember: H₂O: 2 hydrogen + 1 oxygen; CO₂: 1 carbon + 2 oxygen; NaCl: common salt
Heating iron and sulfur forms iron sulfide, which a magnet cannot pull
Compounds have new properties unlike their elements
traps: A magnet or filter cannot split a compound
The small number in a formula belongs to the atom before it
Copper is an element, not a compound

topics.ch: Nature of Matter: Elements, Compounds, and Mixtures
topics.h: A plate of chivda has poha, peanuts, curry leaves and raisins. You can pick out each one. That is the secret of a mixture!
p: A mixture contains two or more substances mixed physically in any proportion. Each substance keeps its own properties.
Mixtures can be separated by physical methods: handpicking, sieving, using a magnet, decanting, filtration and evaporation.
A homogeneous mixture has the same composition throughout, like salt dissolved in water, air, or brass. A heterogeneous mixture is not uniform, like sand in water or oil on water.
Alloys are mixtures of a metal with other elements: brass is copper and zinc; steel is mainly iron with a little carbon.
Elements and compounds are pure substances: they have a fixed composition. Mixtures are not pure substances.

ex.q: Think it through: How would you separate a mixture of salt, sand and iron filings?
st: Move a magnet (wrapped in paper) over it to pull out the iron filings.
Add water and stir: salt dissolves, sand does not.
Filter: sand stays on the filter paper, salt water passes through.
Evaporate the salt water (with an adult, by heating or in sunlight) to get the salt back.
ex.a: Magnet, then dissolving in water, filtration and evaporation.

topics.rl: Salt farmers along the coast of Gujarat let seawater evaporate in shallow pans under the sun, leaving salt behind.

rv.summary: A mixture has two or more substances mixed physically in any proportion, each keeping its properties, so physical methods (sieving, magnet, filtration, evaporation) separate it. Homogeneous mixtures are uniform (salt water, air, brass); heterogeneous ones are not. Elements and compounds are pure.
remember: Brass = copper + zinc; steel = mainly iron + a little carbon
Salt + sand + iron: magnet, dissolve, filter, evaporate
Pure substances: elements and compounds; distilled water is pure
traps: Filtration cannot recover dissolved salt — use evaporation
Air is a mixture, not a compound
Components of a mixture keep their properties and need no fixed ratio

topics.ch: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions
topics.h: Stir sugar into nimbu pani and it vanishes. But taste it and the sweetness is everywhere! Where did the sugar go?
p: When a substance dissolves, it spreads evenly through another substance, forming a solution. A solution is a homogeneous mixture.
The substance that dissolves is the solute (sugar). The substance in which it dissolves is the solvent (water).
Mass is not lost when something dissolves: mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent.
Substances that dissolve in a solvent are soluble (salt, sugar in water). Those that do not are insoluble (sand, chalk powder in water).

Water dissolves so many substances that it is called the universal solvent. Other solvents exist too: nail-polish remover dissolves nail paint, and turpentine dissolves oil paint. Solutions can also hold gases, like carbon dioxide in soda water.

ex.q: Think it through: Arjun dissolves 15 g of salt in 200 g of water. What is the mass of the solution?
st: Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent

topics.rl: The sea is a giant solution: salts are the solutes and water is the solvent. That is why the water tastes salty everywhere you swim.

rv.summary: A solution is a homogeneous mixture of a solute (what dissolves) in a solvent (what dissolves it). Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent. Soluble substances dissolve; insoluble ones like sand do not. Water is the universal solvent; gases like CO₂ can be solutes.
remember: 15 g salt + 200 g water = 215 g solution
Water is the universal solvent, but sand and oil do not dissolve in it
In soda water, CO₂ is the solute
traps: 'Universal solvent' does not mean water dissolves everything
Mass is not lost when something dissolves
The solvent is the larger, dissolving part — not the solute

topics.ch: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions
topics.h: Keep adding sugar to a glass of cold water and a point comes when no more will dissolve. Warm it, and suddenly it can take in more. Why?
p: Solubility is the maximum amount of a solute that can dissolve in a fixed amount of solvent at a given temperature.
A solution in which no more solute can dissolve at that temperature is saturated. If more can still dissolve, it is unsaturated.
For most solids, like sugar, solubility increases when the temperature rises. That is how sugar syrup for gulab jamun is made with hot water.
Gases are less soluble in warm water than in cold water. A warm soda bottle fizzes more when opened, and warm water holds less oxygen for fish.
Stirring and powdering make a solute dissolve faster, but they do not change how much can dissolve (the solubility).

ex.q: Think it through: Sugar stops dissolving in a cup of water at room temperature. Riya warms the cup gently and the leftover sugar dissolves. What does this show?
st: Sugar stopped dissolving, so the solution was saturated at room temperature.
After warming, more sugar dissolved.
So the solubility of sugar increased with temperature.
ex.a: The solubility of sugar increases with temperature; the warm solution can hold more sugar.

topics.rl: Halwais make thick chashni for jalebis by dissolving a lot of sugar in hot water, far more than would dissolve in cold water.

rv.summary: Solubility is the most solute that dissolves in a fixed amount of solvent at a given temperature. A saturated solution can take no more; an unsaturated one can. Most solids dissolve more when hot; gases less. Stirring and powdering speed dissolving but don't change solubility.
focus: Definition of solubility and saturated solutions
Effect of temperature on solids and gases
Speeding up dissolving versus changing solubility
remember: Saturated: no more solute dissolves at that temperature
Hot water dissolves more sugar; warm water holds less gas (oxygen, CO₂)
Stirring and powdering make dissolving faster only
traps: Stirring does not increase solubility
Gases dissolve less, not more, in warm water
Cooling a saturated sugar solution does not let more dissolve

topics.ch: The Amazing World of Solutes, Solvents, and Solutions
topics.h: Two glasses of sharbat look alike, but one tastes much sweeter. Science has a number for that sweetness: concentration!
p: Concentration tells us how much solute is present in a given amount of solution.
A dilute solution has a small amount of solute; a concentrated solution has a large amount. Adding more solvent makes a solution more dilute.
One way to express concentration is mass percentage: (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100.
Remember: mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent.
The right concentration matters. For example, a doctor or a packet's instructions tell exactly how much ORS powder to mix in how much water.

ex.q: Think it through: 20 g of sugar is dissolved in 180 g of water. What is the concentration as a mass percentage?
st: Mass of solution = 20 + 180 = 200 g
Concentration = (20 ÷ 200) × 100

topics.rl: When you add water to a thick mango pulp to make juice, you are diluting it: the same pulp is spread through more water.

rv.summary: Concentration is how much solute is in a given amount of solution. Dilute solutions have little solute and concentrated ones a lot; adding solvent dilutes. Mass percentage = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100, where solution = solute + solvent. Correct concentration matters, as in ORS.
remember: Mass % = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100
20 g sugar + 180 g water = 200 g solution → 10%
Adding water lowers concentration
traps: Divide by the mass of solution, not the mass of solvent
More powder in ORS is not better

topics.t: Reflection and images in a plane mirror
topics.h: Why is the word AMBULANCE written backwards on the front of an ambulance? A mirror holds the answer!
p: When light falls on a shiny surface and bounces back, it is called reflection. The ray hitting the mirror is the incident ray; the ray bouncing off is the reflected ray.
The normal is a line drawn at 90° to the mirror where the ray strikes it. Angles are measured from the normal.
Law of reflection: the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. The incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal all lie in the same plane.
A plane mirror forms an image that is erect (upright), the same size as the object, and as far behind the mirror as the object is in front.
The image is virtual (it cannot be caught on a screen) and laterally inverted: left and right appear swapped.

ex.q: Think it through: A ray of light makes an angle of 30° with the surface of a plane mirror. What is the angle of reflection?
st: Angles are measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the mirror.
Angle of incidence = 90° − 30° = 60°.
Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 60°.

topics.rl: AMBULANCE is printed in mirror writing so that drivers ahead read it correctly in their rear-view mirrors and make way.

rv.summary: Reflection is light bouncing off a shiny surface. Angles are measured from the normal (90° to the mirror), and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection. A plane mirror's image is virtual, erect, the same size, as far behind as the object is in front, and laterally inverted.
focus: Incident ray, reflected ray and the normal
remember: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection, measured from the normal
Ray at 30° to the mirror surface → angle of incidence 60°
Plane mirror image: virtual, erect, same size, laterally inverted
traps: Measure angles from the normal, not from the mirror surface
A ray along the normal has angle 0°, not 90°
A virtual image cannot be caught on a screen

topics.h: Look into a shiny steel spoon. The inside shows you upside down, and the back shows you tiny and upright. One spoon, two kinds of mirrors!
p: Spherical mirrors are curved like part of a hollow ball. A concave mirror curves inward (like the inside of a spoon); a convex mirror bulges outward (like the back of a spoon).
A concave mirror makes an object placed very close to it look bigger, erect and virtual. For a far object it forms an inverted image that is real and can be caught on a screen.
Concave mirrors are used in torches and vehicle headlights (to send out a strong beam), as shaving and dentists' mirrors, and in solar cookers to concentrate sunlight.
A convex mirror always forms an erect, smaller (diminished) and virtual image, and shows a wide area.
Convex mirrors are used as rear-view mirrors in vehicles and at sharp turns on hill roads so drivers can see what is coming.

ex.q: Think it through: A dentist holds a small curved mirror close to a tooth and sees a bigger upright image. Which kind of mirror is it?
st: The image is bigger (enlarged) and upright.
A convex mirror always makes images smaller, so it is not convex.
A concave mirror gives an enlarged, erect image when the object is very close.
ex.a: A concave mirror.

topics.rl: On winding ghat roads in places like Munnar or Shimla, large convex mirrors at bends let drivers see vehicles coming around the corner.

rv.summary: Concave mirrors curve inward; convex mirrors bulge outward. Concave mirrors enlarge close objects, form real images of far ones, and are used in torches, headlights, shaving mirrors and solar cookers. Convex mirrors always give erect, smaller, virtual images and a wide view.
remember: Concave: torch, headlights, shaving and dentist's mirrors, solar cooker
Convex: rear-view mirrors, sharp bends on hill roads
Convex mirror image is always erect, smaller and virtual
traps: An enlarged image means concave, never convex
The inside of a spoon is concave; the back is convex
Only a concave mirror (not plane or convex) forms a real image on a screen

topics.t: Lenses and the images they form
topics.h: Your grandparents' reading glasses, a phone camera and a school microscope all work because of a curved piece of glass called a lens!
p: A lens is a piece of transparent material with at least one curved surface. Light bends (refracts) as it passes through it.
A convex lens is thicker in the middle than at the edges. It brings parallel rays of light together (converging lens).
A convex lens held close to an object gives an enlarged, erect, virtual image: this is a magnifying glass. For a distant object, it forms a real, inverted image on a screen.
A concave lens is thinner in the middle than at the edges. It spreads light rays apart (diverging lens) and always forms an erect, smaller, virtual image.
Lenses are used in spectacles, cameras, microscopes, telescopes and projectors. Safety: never look at the Sun through a lens, and never use a lens to focus sunlight on anything, as it can burn.

ex.q: Think it through: Anjali holds a lens between a bright window and a white wall and sees a small, upside-down picture of the window on the wall. Which lens is it?
st: The image is caught on the wall, so it is a real image.
It is inverted, which happens for a real image from a convex lens.
A concave lens always gives virtual images, which cannot be caught on a wall.
ex.a: A convex lens.

topics.rl: Jewellers and watch repairers use a convex lens (an eyepiece magnifier) to see tiny details. Spectacles for people who cannot see far clearly use concave lenses.

rv.summary: A lens bends (refracts) light. A convex lens, thicker in the middle, converges rays: it magnifies close objects and forms real, inverted images of far ones. A concave lens, thinner in the middle, diverges rays and always gives erect, smaller, virtual images. Never look at the Sun through a lens.
focus: Uses of lenses and lens safety
remember: Convex lens: converging, magnifying glass, real image on a screen
Concave lens: diverging, always erect, smaller, virtual
Used in spectacles, cameras, microscopes, telescopes, projectors
traps: Refraction is bending; reflection is bouncing back
A concave lens can never form an image on a screen
Never look at the Sun or focus sunlight on anything with a lens

topics.t: Day, month and year from the sky
topics.h: Long before clocks and phones, people knew when to sow seeds and when to celebrate harvests just by watching the Sun, the Moon and the stars!
p: A day comes from the Earth spinning on its axis (rotation). From one sunrise to the next takes about 24 hours.
A month comes from the Moon's phases. From one new moon to the next takes about 29.5 days.
A year comes from the Earth going once around the Sun (revolution). It takes about 365¼ days, so every fourth year gets an extra day, 29 February: a leap year.
Through the year the Sun's rising point on the horizon slowly shifts north and south, and the length of shadows at noon changes. People used sticks (gnomons) and sundials to track this.

In the northern half of the Earth, the longest day comes around 21 June (summer solstice) and the shortest around 22 December (winter solstice). Around 21 March and 23 September (equinoxes), day and night are nearly equal.

ex.q: Think it through: A calendar year has 365 days, but the Earth takes about 365¼ days to go around the Sun. What would happen if we never added leap days?
st: Each year the calendar would fall about ¼ day behind the Earth's actual position.
After 4 years that adds up to about 1 day.
Over a few centuries the dates would drift by weeks, and seasons would arrive in the 'wrong' months.
ex.a: The calendar would slowly drift away from the seasons, so we add a leap day roughly every four years.

topics.rl: The Jantar Mantar in Jaipur, built in the 1700s, has a giant sundial whose shadow tells the local time, a reminder of how India tracked time using the sky.

rv.summary: A day comes from the Earth's rotation (24 hours), a month from the Moon's phases (29.5 days) and a year from its revolution around the Sun (365¼ days), so every fourth year adds 29 February. Solstices (21 June, 22 December) give the longest and shortest days; at equinoxes day equals night.
focus: Day, month and year from rotation, Moon and revolution
Changing noon shadows and the gnomon
remember: Day ≈ 24 hours; lunar month ≈ 29.5 days; year ≈ 365¼ days
Leap year: divisible by 4, February has 29 days
Longest day ~21 June, shortest ~22 December; equinoxes ~21 March and 23 September
traps: Day and night come from rotation, not revolution
Noon shadows are shorter in summer, longer in winter
Without leap days the calendar would drift from the seasons

topics.h: The Moon seems to grow from a thin silver smile into a full round plate and then shrink away again. But it never really changes shape!
p: The Moon has no light of its own. It shines because it reflects sunlight, and the half facing the Sun is always lit.
As the Moon goes around the Earth, we see different amounts of its lit half. These changing shapes are called phases.

Order of phases: new moon (Amavasya, Moon not visible), waxing crescent, first quarter (half moon), waxing gibbous, full moon (Purnima), waning gibbous, last quarter, waning crescent, and back to new moon.
The bright part grows (waxes) for about 15 days from new moon to full moon, called Shukla Paksha in many Indian calendars, and shrinks (wanes) for about 15 days, called Krishna Paksha.
The full cycle takes about 29.5 days. The Moon also rises about 50 minutes later each day, on average; a full moon rises around sunset.

ex.q: Think it through: Tonight is full moon. About how many days until the next full moon, and what phase will you see after about a week?
st: One complete cycle of phases takes about 29.5 days.
After full moon, the lit part starts shrinking (waning).
About a week later the Moon is half lit: the last quarter.
ex.a: About 29.5 days until the next full moon; after about a week you will see the last quarter (a half moon).

topics.rl: Many Indian festivals are fixed by the Moon: some fall on a full-moon night and others on a new-moon night, which is why their dates change from year to year.

rv.summary: The Moon shines by reflected sunlight; half of it is always lit. As it orbits the Earth we see changing amounts of the lit half: the phases, from new moon (Amavasya) to full moon (Purnima) and back. The cycle takes about 29.5 days, and the Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day.
focus: Why the Moon shines and shows phases
remember: New moon → waxing crescent → first quarter → waxing gibbous → full moon → waning gibbous → last quarter → waning crescent
Cycle ≈ 29.5 days; full moon rises around sunset
Shukla Paksha: waxing; Krishna Paksha: waning
traps: Phases are not caused by the Earth's shadow
The Moon does not change its shape or make its own light
Moonrise is about 50 minutes later each day, not at the same time

topics.h: Why does a festival fall in October one year and November the next, while your birthday stays on the same date every year? Different calendars!
p: A solar calendar follows the Sun and the seasons. The Gregorian calendar we use for school and work is solar, with 365 days and 366 in a leap year.
A lunar calendar follows the Moon. Twelve lunar months of about 29.5 days make about 354 days, roughly 11 days shorter than a solar year.
So in a purely lunar calendar, dates slowly shift through the seasons. The Hijri calendar is an example of a lunar calendar.

A lunisolar calendar uses lunar months but adds an extra month about every two and a half to three years to keep in step with the seasons. Many traditional Indian calendars do this; the extra month is called Adhik Maas.
India's national calendar, the Saka calendar, was adopted in 1957. Its first month, Chaitra, usually begins on 22 March (21 March in a leap year).

ex.q: Think it through: How many days shorter is a 12-month lunar year than a 365-day solar year? (Take a lunar month as 29.5 days.)
st: Lunar year = 12 × 29.5 = 354 days
Difference = 365 − 354 = 11 days
ex.a: About 11 days

topics.rl: Wall calendars in many Indian homes show both the Gregorian date and the tithi from a traditional calendar, so families can plan both school days and festivals.

rv.summary: Solar calendars like the Gregorian follow the seasons (365 or 366 days). Lunar calendars like the Hijri have 12 months of about 29.5 days, about 354 days, so dates drift about 11 days a year. Lunisolar calendars add Adhik Maas. India's Saka calendar (1957) starts with Chaitra on 22 March.
focus: Why lunar dates drift by about 11 days
remember: Lunar year = 12 × 29.5 = 354 days, about 11 days shorter than 365
Saka calendar adopted 1957; first month Chaitra, usually from 22 March
Adhik Maas added about every 2½–3 years
traps: The Gregorian calendar is solar, not lunisolar
A purely lunar calendar adds no extra month
The Saka calendar was adopted in 1957, not 1947

topics.h: A small village pond has fish, frogs, water lilies, dragonflies, sunlight, mud and water, all working together like one big team!
p: An ecosystem is a community of living things interacting with each other and with the non-living things around them.
Living (biotic) parts include plants, animals and microorganisms. Non-living (abiotic) parts include sunlight, air, water, soil, minerals and temperature.
Ecosystems can be large or small: a forest, a grassland, a desert, a pond, a sea, or even a rotting log.
India has many ecosystems: the mangrove forests of the Sundarbans, the rainforests of the Western Ghats, the Thar Desert and Chilika Lake in Odisha.
The living things in an ecosystem are suited (adapted) to its non-living conditions, like camels to the hot, dry desert.

ex.q: Think it through: In a school garden there are neem trees, earthworms, sparrows, soil, sunlight and rainwater. Sort them into living and non-living parts of the ecosystem.
st: Living things grow, need food and reproduce: neem trees, earthworms and sparrows.
Non-living parts do not do these things: soil, sunlight and rainwater.
Together, and interacting, they form the garden ecosystem.
ex.a: Living: neem trees, earthworms, sparrows. Non-living: soil, sunlight, rainwater.

topics.rl: Mangrove forests in the Sundarbans protect the coast from storms and are home to the Royal Bengal tiger, crabs, fish and many birds.

rv.summary: An ecosystem is living things (plants, animals, microbes) interacting with each other and with non-living parts (sunlight, air, water, soil). It can be a forest or a rotting log. India has the Sundarbans, Western Ghats, Thar Desert and Chilika Lake; organisms are adapted to their conditions.
remember: Biotic: plants, animals, microorganisms; abiotic: sunlight, air, water, soil, minerals, temperature
Sundarbans: largest mangrove forest
Camels are adapted to the hot, dry Thar Desert
traps: Water and sunlight are non-living parts, not living
Ecosystems need not be big — a log counts
Fungi are living, even though they are not plants or animals

topics.h: The energy in the muscles of a tiger chasing a deer in Kanha started out as sunlight falling on a blade of grass!
p: Green plants are producers: they make their own food from sunlight, water and carbon dioxide (photosynthesis).
Consumers eat other living things. Herbivores eat plants (deer), carnivores eat animals (tiger), and omnivores eat both (bear, crow, humans).
A food chain shows who eats whom, with arrows pointing towards the eater: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle.
Energy passes along the chain, but much of it is used for living and lost as heat at each step. Only a small part (about 10%) passes to the next level, so food chains are usually short.
In nature, food chains link together to form a food web. Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead remains at every level and return nutrients to the soil.

ex.q: Think it through: In the chain grass → deer → tiger, which is the producer, which is the herbivore and which is the carnivore? Where does the energy begin?
st: Grass makes its own food using sunlight: producer.
The deer eats grass: herbivore (primary consumer).
The tiger eats deer: carnivore (secondary consumer).
The energy begins with sunlight captured by the grass.
ex.a: Grass is the producer, deer the herbivore and tiger the carnivore; the energy comes from the Sun.

topics.rl: A garden with many kinds of plants supports more insects, birds and lizards, because many food chains link into a strong food web.

rv.summary: Green plants are producers. Consumers are herbivores, carnivores or omnivores. A food chain shows who eats whom, with arrows towards the eater. Only about 10% of energy passes to the next level, so chains are short. Linked chains form a food web, and decomposers recycle nutrients.
focus: Reading a food chain and its arrows
remember: Grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → eagle
About 10% of energy passes to the next level
Omnivores: bear, crow, humans; decomposers: bacteria and fungi
traps: Arrows point towards the eater, not the food
Mushrooms are decomposers, not producers
Most energy is lost as heat at each step, not passed on

topics.h: No bees, no mangoes? It is true! Many fruit trees need bees and other insects to carry pollen from flower to flower.
p: Living things depend on each other for food, shelter, pollination and seed dispersal. This is called interdependence.
Plants give oxygen and food; animals breathe out carbon dioxide that plants use. Bees and butterflies pollinate flowers, and birds and animals spread seeds.
Decomposers break down dead matter, recycling nutrients so new plants can grow.
If one population changes, others are affected. If frogs disappear from a field, insects may increase while snakes that eat frogs may decrease.
A balanced ecosystem has many kinds of living things. Human activities like cutting forests, pollution and overfishing can upset this balance.

ex.q: Think it through: Farmers in a village kill most of the snakes in their fields. What might happen to the rats, and to the crops?
st: Snakes eat rats.
With fewer snakes, fewer rats are eaten, so the rat population grows.
More rats eat more grain, so crop damage increases.
ex.a: Rats would increase and damage more crops, showing how removing one species upsets the balance.

topics.rl: When vulture numbers fell sharply in India, dead animals were left lying for longer. Vultures are nature's clean-up crew, so their loss affected the whole ecosystem.

rv.summary: Living things depend on each other (interdependence) for food, shelter, gases, pollination and seed dispersal; decomposers recycle nutrients. If one population changes, others are affected: without frogs, insects rise and snakes fall. Deforestation, pollution and overfishing upset the balance.
remember: Bees pollinate; birds disperse seeds
No frogs → more insects, fewer snakes; fewer snakes → more rats
Plants give oxygen, animals give carbon dioxide
traps: Losing a predator makes its prey increase, not decrease
Vultures are scavengers, not producers
Planting native trees helps balance; it does not upset it

topics.ch: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet
topics.t: What makes life possible on Earth
topics.h: Venus is hotter than an oven and Mars is a freezing desert. Earth, the third planet from the Sun, is 'just right'. Out of all the planets we know, only Earth is known to have life!
p: Earth is at a suitable distance from the Sun, so it is neither too hot nor too cold, and water can stay liquid on its surface.
Liquid water covers about 71% of Earth's surface. All living things need water. But about 97% of Earth's water is salty sea water, and most fresh water is frozen as ice.
Earth's atmosphere gives us oxygen to breathe and carbon dioxide for plants. It also traps some heat, keeping Earth's average temperature comfortable, about 15 °C.
The ozone layer high in the atmosphere absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays.
Earth also has fertile soil for plants, and a magnetic field that helps shield it from harmful particles streaming from the Sun.

ex.q: Think it through: Why is liquid water so important when scientists search for life on other planets?
st: Every living thing on Earth needs water to survive.
Water dissolves nutrients and carries them in living bodies.
So a planet with liquid water is more likely to support life as we know it.
ex.a: All known life needs liquid water, so it is one of the first things scientists look for.

topics.rl: ISRO's Chandrayaan-1 mission (2008) helped find signs of water on the Moon, showing how important the search for water is in space science.

rv.summary: Earth is at a suitable distance from the Sun, so water stays liquid; water covers about 71% of its surface, but about 97% is salty and most fresh water is ice. The atmosphere gives oxygen and keeps Earth warm (about 15 °C), the ozone layer blocks UV rays, and the magnetic field shields it.
focus: Distance from the Sun and liquid water
remember: Water covers about 71% of the surface; land about 29%
About 97% of water is salty; most fresh water is frozen
Ozone layer absorbs UV rays; average temperature about 15 °C
traps: 97% is the salty share of water, not the share of surface covered
Earth is the third planet, not the second
The ozone layer blocks UV rays; it does not make oxygen for breathing

topics.ch: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet
topics.t: Our air and the ozone shield
topics.h: Every breath you take is a mixture of gases, and only about one-fifth of it is the oxygen your body needs!
p: Air is a mixture of gases: about 78% nitrogen, about 21% oxygen, and about 1% other gases such as argon, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
Oxygen is used by most living things to get energy from food. Carbon dioxide, though only about 0.04% of air, is used by plants to make food.
Some gases, like carbon dioxide and methane, trap heat. This natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm, but adding too much of these gases is warming Earth more and changing the climate.

The ozone layer can be damaged by chemicals called CFCs, once used in old refrigerators and sprays. Countries agreed in the Montreal Protocol (1987) to phase them out, and the ozone layer is slowly recovering.
Burning fuels, smoke from vehicles and burning waste pollute the air and can harm our lungs. Clean air is essential for good health.

ex.q: Think it through: If air contains about 21% oxygen, how many litres of oxygen are in 100 litres of air?
st: 21% means 21 parts out of 100.
21% of 100 litres = 21 litres.
ex.a: About 21 litres

topics.rl: During winter, cities in north India sometimes face heavy smog. Air Quality Index (AQI) boards and apps help people know when to stay indoors.

rv.summary: Air is about 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 1% other gases, including about 0.04% carbon dioxide used by plants. Greenhouse gases keep Earth warm, but too much warms it further. CFCs damaged the ozone layer; the Montreal Protocol (1987) phased them out. Burning fuels and waste pollutes the air.
focus: CFCs, ozone damage and the Montreal Protocol
remember: Nitrogen ~78%, oxygen ~21%, others ~1%; CO₂ ~0.04%
Montreal Protocol 1987 phased out CFCs
21% of 100 litres of air = 21 litres of oxygen
traps: Oxygen is not the largest part of air — nitrogen is
CFCs thin the ozone layer; they don't thicken it
Some greenhouse effect is natural and needed

topics.ch: Our Home: Earth, a Unique Life Sustaining Planet
topics.h: There is no Planet B! But small daily choices, like carrying a cloth bag, can add up to a big difference for Earth.
p: Earth faces problems like air and water pollution, plastic waste, cutting of forests, loss of wild species and climate change.
Biodiversity means the variety of living things in a place. Protecting it keeps ecosystems healthy and balanced.
India protects wildlife through national parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves. Project Tiger, started in 1973, helped protect tigers and their forests.
Communities have also protected nature. In the Chipko movement of the 1970s in the Himalayan region, villagers hugged trees to stop them from being cut.
We can help by following the 3Rs: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle; by saving water and electricity, segregating wet and dry waste, planting native trees, and using public transport or cycling.

ex.q: Think it through: Your family uses about 5 plastic bags a day. If you switch to cloth bags, how many plastic bags will you avoid in one week?
st: Bags per day = 5
Days in a week = 7
ex.a: 35 plastic bags in a week

topics.rl: Many Indian cities ask homes to give wet waste and dry waste separately. Wet waste can become compost and dry waste can be recycled.

rv.summary: Earth faces pollution, plastic waste, deforestation, species loss and climate change. Biodiversity keeps ecosystems healthy. India protects wildlife in national parks, sanctuaries and biosphere reserves; Project Tiger began in 1973 and the Chipko movement saved trees. We help through the 3Rs.
remember: Project Tiger: 1973
Chipko (1970s, Himalayan region): villagers hugged trees
3Rs: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle; e.g. 5 bags a day × 7 = 35 bags saved a week
traps: Reusing a jar is reuse, not recycling
Burning garbage pollutes; it does not enrich the soil
Idling engines and driving alone increase pollution

qa.q: Which of these is a testable hypothesis?
qa.a: Salt water makes ice melt faster than plain water.
qa.e: We can test this by putting the same ice cubes in salt water and plain water and timing them. The other options are opinions that cannot be measured.

qa.q: Meera notices that her bicycle tyre looks flatter in winter. What is this first step called?
qa.e: Noticing something with our senses is an observation. Investigations usually start with one.

qa.q: Why should an experiment be repeated several times?
qa.a: To make the result more reliable
qa.e: Repeating checks that the result was not just luck or a mistake in one trial.

qa.q: Kabir's results do not support his hypothesis. What should he do?
qa.a: Accept the results and think of a new hypothesis to test
