qa.e: Honest results that disagree with a hypothesis help us improve our idea. Science moves forward this way.

qa.q: What is 'data' in an investigation?
qa.a: The observations and measurements we record
qa.e: Data are the observations and measurements collected during an investigation, such as heights, times or temperatures.

qa.q: Which step comes right after making a hypothesis?
qa.e: Once we have a hypothesis, we design and carry out an experiment to test it.

qa.q: Why do scientists share their results with others?
qa.a: So others can check and build on the work
qa.e: When others repeat and check the work, mistakes are caught and knowledge grows.

qa.q: Priya keeps a table of the daily temperature and the time milk takes to set into curd. Which step is she doing?
qa.e: Writing measurements in a table is recording data, which she will later analyse.

qa.q: Rohan tests whether the height of a ramp changes how far a toy car rolls. What is the independent variable?
qa.e: Rohan changes the ramp height on purpose, so it is the independent variable. The distance is what he measures.

qa.q: In the same ramp test, what is the dependent variable?
qa.e: The distance depends on the ramp height, and it is what Rohan measures.

qa.q: Why must we change only one variable at a time?
qa.a: So that we know which change caused the result
qa.e: If two things change together, we cannot tell which one caused the difference in the results.

qa.q: Neha tests which detergent removes a turmeric stain best. Which should she keep the SAME for every cloth?
qa.a: The size of the stain and the washing time
qa.e: To be fair, only the detergent changes. Stain size, cloth, water and washing time must stay the same.

qa.q: A student grows one plant with fertiliser and one plant without it. What is the plant without fertiliser called?
qa.e: The plant without the change is the control. We compare the fertilised plant with it.

qa.q: Which experiment is a fair test of whether sunlight helps seeds sprout?
qa.a: One tray in sunlight and one in the dark, both with the same water, soil and seeds
qa.e: Only the light is different, so any difference in sprouting can be linked to light.

qa.q: Anil wants to know if the mass of a pendulum bob affects how long one swing takes. Which is a controlled variable?
qa.e: He changes the mass and measures the swing time, so the string length must be kept the same.

qa.q: Why do scientists usually test many seeds instead of just one in each tray?
qa.a: One seed may behave unusually, so more seeds give a reliable result
qa.e: A single seed might be damaged. Using many seeds gives a result we can trust more.

qa.q: Which of these is a fungus?
qa.e: Yeast is a single-celled fungus. Amoeba is a protozoan, Lactobacillus a bacterium and Spirogyra an alga.

qa.q: Which group of microbes can multiply only inside the cells of another living thing?
qa.e: Viruses do not multiply on their own. They use the host's cells to make copies of themselves.

qa.q: Why do we need a microscope to see bacteria?
qa.a: Bacteria are far too small for our eyes
qa.e: Bacteria are only a few micrometres long, so a microscope must magnify them for us to see them.

qa.q: Amoeba belongs to which group?
qa.e: Amoeba is a single-celled protozoan that moves with false feet.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a microorganism?
qa.e: An earthworm is easily seen with the naked eye. Paramecium, bread mould and Lactobacillus are all microorganisms.

qa.q: Green slimy growth in a pond is most likely made of:
qa.e: Algae contain chlorophyll, which makes them green. They grow well in still water with sunlight.

qa.q: Which statement about where microbes live is correct?
qa.a: Almost everywhere, including soil, water, air and our bodies
qa.e: Microbes are found nearly everywhere, even inside our intestines, where many help us.

qa.q: Which microbe group includes many-celled forms such as mushrooms and moulds?
qa.e: Fungi include single-celled yeast and many-celled moulds and mushrooms.

qa.q: Who first used the word 'cell' after looking at cork?
qa.e: Robert Hooke studied a thin slice of cork in 1665 and called the tiny boxes cells.

qa.q: In which year did Robert Hooke describe cells in cork?
qa.e: Hooke published his observations of cork cells in 1665.

qa.q: Which part is found in a plant cell but NOT in an animal cell?
qa.e: Plant cells have a cell wall outside the cell membrane. Animal cells have only a cell membrane.

qa.q: Which part of the cell controls its activities?
qa.e: The nucleus is the control centre of the cell.

qa.q: A microscope has a 10× eyepiece and a 10× objective. How many times bigger does the specimen appear?
qa.e: Magnifications of the two lenses are multiplied, not added.

qa.q: Amoeba is called unicellular because:
qa.a: It is made of one cell
qa.e: Uni means one. An Amoeba's whole body is just one cell that does all life activities.

qa.q: Green chloroplasts are found in the cells of:
qa.e: Leaf cells have chloroplasts that capture sunlight to make food. Animal cells do not have them.

qa.q: Which correctly lists levels from smaller to larger?
qa.e: Similar cells form a tissue, and different tissues together form an organ.

qa.q: Which microbe helps convert milk into curd?
qa.e: Lactobacillus bacteria multiply in milk and turn it into curd.

qa.q: Why does idli batter rise when kept overnight?
qa.a: Microbes ferment it and release carbon dioxide gas
qa.e: Fermenting microbes make carbon dioxide, and its bubbles make the batter rise and soft.

qa.q: Rhizobium bacteria help plants by:
qa.a: Fixing nitrogen from the air into the soil
qa.e: Rhizobium lives in root nodules of legumes and converts nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use.

qa.q: Who discovered penicillin?
qa.e: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin from a Penicillium mould in 1928.

qa.q: Antibiotics will NOT cure which of these?
qa.e: The common cold is caused by viruses, and antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses.

qa.q: Malaria is caused by:
qa.e: Malaria is caused by the protozoan Plasmodium, which is spread by the bite of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes.

qa.q: What do decomposer microbes do in a compost pit?
qa.e: Decomposers break down plant and food waste into compost that enriches soil. They cannot break down most plastics.

qa.q: Why do pickles made with lots of salt last for months?
qa.a: Salt removes water so most microbes cannot grow
qa.e: Salt draws water out of food and microbes, so they cannot grow and spoil the pickle.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-communicable disease?
qa.e: Diabetes does not pass from one person to another. The others are infections caused by pathogens.

qa.q: Dengue is spread by:
qa.e: Dengue virus is carried from person to person by the bite of infected Aedes mosquitoes.

qa.q: Which mosquito spreads malaria?
qa.e: Only female mosquitoes bite to feed on blood, and infected female Anopheles mosquitoes pass on the malaria parasite.

qa.q: A carrier, like a mosquito, that spreads a pathogen is called a:
qa.e: A vector carries pathogens from one host to another without being the cause itself.

qa.q: Tuberculosis mainly spreads through:
qa.a: Air when an infected person coughs or sneezes
qa.e: TB bacteria are released into the air in tiny droplets when an infected person coughs or sneezes.

qa.q: Which of these best describes good health?
qa.e: Health includes the body, the mind and how we get along with others.

qa.q: Cholera and typhoid usually spread through:
qa.e: The bacteria that cause them enter the body through dirty water or food.

qa.q: Why can't you 'catch' heart disease from a friend?
qa.a: It is non-communicable and not caused by a pathogen that spreads
qa.e: Heart disease is linked to lifestyle, diet, age and family history, not to a germ passed between people.

qa.q: Which action best stops mosquitoes from breeding at home?
qa.a: Emptying and cleaning water coolers and pots regularly
qa.e: Mosquitoes lay eggs in still water, so removing it stops them from breeding.

qa.q: Why should we cover our mouth while coughing?
qa.a: To stop droplets carrying germs from spreading
qa.e: Coughs release tiny droplets that can carry pathogens to others nearby.

qa.q: Which is the safest way to make river water fit for drinking at home?
qa.a: Boil it or use a water purifier
qa.e: Boiling or proper purification kills or removes most pathogens.

qa.q: A lack of vitamin C in the diet causes:
qa.e: Scurvy, with bleeding gums, is a deficiency disease. Amla, guava, lemon and oranges are rich in vitamin C.

qa.q: Which habit helps prevent non-communicable diseases like diabetes?
qa.a: Regular exercise and a balanced diet
qa.e: Lifestyle diseases are reduced by staying active and eating healthy food.

qa.q: When is it most important to wash hands with soap?
qa.a: Before eating and after using the toilet
qa.e: Germs on hands can enter the mouth while eating. Hands can carry germs even if they look clean.

qa.q: Which of these can carry typhoid germs onto food, and is kept away by covering the food?
qa.e: Houseflies can carry germs from waste to uncovered food, so covering food protects us.

qa.q: Which food is a good source of vitamin C?
qa.e: Amla (Indian gooseberry) is one of the richest natural sources of vitamin C.

qa.q: What does a vaccine contain?
qa.a: Weakened or killed germs, or harmless parts of them
qa.e: A vaccine safely teaches the immune system to recognise a germ without making you ill.

qa.q: Who developed the first vaccine, against smallpox?
qa.e: Edward Jenner developed the smallpox vaccine in 1796.

qa.q: In which year was smallpox declared eradicated worldwide?
qa.e: The World Health Organization declared smallpox eradicated in 1980 after a global vaccination campaign.

qa.q: In which year was India certified polio-free?
qa.e: India was certified polio-free in 2014 after years of the Pulse Polio campaign.

qa.q: Which cells of the body fight pathogens?
qa.e: White blood cells are the immune system's defenders and make antibodies.

qa.q: Rahul has the flu, which is caused by a virus. Why is an antibiotic not the right medicine for the virus?
qa.a: Antibiotics act on bacteria, not viruses
qa.e: Antibiotics kill or stop bacteria. They do not work on viruses, so a doctor decides what is needed.

qa.q: Why should a full course of antibiotics be taken exactly as the doctor says?
qa.a: Stopping early can leave bacteria that become resistant
qa.e: Misusing antibiotics helps resistant bacteria survive and spread, making future infections harder to treat.

qa.q: When many people in a community are vaccinated, even those who cannot be vaccinated are better protected. Why?
qa.a: The germ finds fewer people to spread through
qa.e: If most people are immune, a germ cannot easily pass from person to person, so everyone is safer.

qa.q: Who discovered that an electric current affects a compass needle?
qa.e: Oersted observed in 1820 that a current-carrying wire deflects a nearby compass needle.

qa.q: In which year did Oersted report the magnetic effect of current?
qa.e: Oersted's discovery was made and reported in 1820.

qa.q: A compass needle near a wire deflects only when the switch is ON. What does this show?
qa.a: A current produces a magnetic field
qa.e: The needle responds to the magnetic field that exists only while current flows.

qa.q: What happens to the compass deflection if the current direction is reversed?
qa.a: The needle deflects in the opposite direction
qa.e: Reversing the current reverses the magnetic field, so the needle turns the other way.

qa.q: Why is a coil better than a straight wire for showing the magnetic effect?
qa.a: A coil makes the magnetic effect stronger
qa.e: In a coil, the magnetic fields of all the turns add up, giving a stronger effect.

qa.q: A current-carrying coil behaves most like:
qa.e: It has a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other, like a bar magnet.

qa.q: Which household appliance uses the magnetic effect of current in its motor?
qa.e: The fan's electric motor uses current-carrying coils that act like magnets to make it spin.

qa.q: What is the safest power source for a school compass-and-wire experiment?
qa.a: A dry cell with a switch
qa.e: Dry cells give a small, safe current. Mains electricity can give a dangerous shock.

qa.q: What is an electromagnet made of?
qa.a: A coil of insulated wire around an iron core
qa.e: Current through the coil magnetises the iron core.

qa.q: When does an electromagnet act as a magnet?
qa.a: Only while current flows through its coil
qa.e: Switch off the current and the soft iron core loses most of its magnetism.

qa.q: Which change will make an electromagnet stronger?
qa.e: More turns add up their magnetic effects, making a stronger magnet.

qa.q: Why does a scrapyard use an electromagnet instead of a permanent magnet?
qa.a: It can be switched off to drop the scrap
qa.e: Switching off the current releases the load, which a permanent magnet cannot do.

qa.q: How can you reverse the poles of an electromagnet?
qa.a: Reverse the direction of the current
qa.e: The poles depend on the current's direction, so reversing the current swaps them.

qa.q: Which of these uses an electromagnet?
qa.e: In an electric bell, an electromagnet repeatedly pulls a metal strip to ring the gong.

qa.q: Which material is best for the core of an electromagnet?
qa.e: Soft iron becomes strongly magnetic while current flows and loses its magnetism quickly when switched off.

qa.q: Why must the wire in an electromagnet be insulated?
qa.a: So current flows around every turn instead of jumping across touching turns
qa.e: If bare turns touched, current would take a short path and the coil would not work properly.

qa.q: Which appliance works mainly on the heating effect of current?
qa.e: An electric iron has a heating element that gets hot when current flows.

qa.q: What is the job of a fuse in a circuit?
qa.a: To melt and break the circuit when the current is too large
qa.e: A fuse protects wiring and appliances by cutting the circuit when too much current flows.

qa.q: Why is a fuse wire made of a material with a low melting point?
qa.a: So it melts quickly when the current is too large
qa.e: It must melt before the house wiring gets dangerously hot.

qa.q: Which material is commonly used for the heating element of a room heater?
qa.e: Nichrome gets very hot when current flows but does not melt or burn easily.

qa.q: Why do LED bulbs save electricity compared with filament bulbs?
qa.a: They waste much less energy as heat
qa.e: A filament bulb turns most of its energy into heat. An LED turns much more into light.

qa.q: The filament of an old-style bulb is made of:
qa.e: Tungsten has a very high melting point, so it can glow white-hot without melting.

qa.q: What does an MCB do?
qa.a: Switches off the circuit automatically when the current is too large
qa.e: An MCB (miniature circuit breaker) does the job of a fuse and can be switched back on after the fault is fixed.

qa.q: Which is a safe habit with electric heating appliances?
qa.a: Switching off and unplugging the iron after use
qa.e: Unplugging after use prevents overheating and accidents. The other actions are dangerous.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of force?
qa.e: Force is measured in newtons (N), named after Isaac Newton.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-contact force?
qa.e: A magnet can pull iron without touching it, so magnetic force acts from a distance.

qa.q: A rubbed balloon sticks to a wall. Which force is mainly at work?
qa.e: Rubbing charges the balloon, and charged objects attract other objects through the electrostatic force.

qa.q: Which effect of force is seen when you press a ball of atta dough?
qa.e: A force can change the shape of an object, as when dough flattens.

qa.q: A mug of water feels lighter when it is still under water in a bucket. Why?
qa.e: Water exerts an upward buoyant force, so we need less force to hold the mug.

qa.q: Which force pulls a ripe mango down to the ground?
qa.e: The Earth's gravity pulls all objects towards it, even without touching them.

qa.q: A force always has:
qa.a: Both a size and a direction
qa.e: To describe a force fully, we must say how strong it is and in which direction it acts.

qa.q: A batsman hits a ball coming towards him back towards the bowler. The main change in the ball's motion is:
qa.e: The bat's force reverses the ball's direction of motion.

qa.q: Friction always acts:
qa.a: Opposite to the relative motion between the surfaces
qa.e: Friction opposes the sliding or rolling of one surface over another.

qa.q: Why do tyres have treads?
qa.a: To increase friction and grip on the road
qa.e: Treads grip the road better, so vehicles do not skid, especially on wet roads.

qa.q: Which reduces friction in the moving parts of a sewing machine?
qa.e: Oil is a lubricant. It forms a thin layer that lets parts slide smoothly.

qa.q: Why do we slip on a wet, soapy floor?
qa.e: The soapy water fills the tiny bumps on the floor, reducing friction between our feet and the floor.

qa.q: Which is the easiest way to move a heavy gas cylinder across a floor?
qa.e: Rolling friction is smaller than sliding friction. (Gas cylinders should be moved only by adults.)

qa.q: Why do aeroplanes, fast trains and fish have pointed, smooth shapes?
qa.a: To reduce drag from air or water
qa.e: Streamlined shapes let air or water flow around them smoothly, reducing the opposing force.

qa.q: What is a disadvantage of friction?
qa.a: It wears out shoe soles and machine parts
qa.e: Rubbing slowly wears away surfaces and wastes energy as heat.

qa.q: Which surface gives the most friction to a rolling marble?
qa.e: Rough surfaces have more bumps that resist motion, so the marble stops sooner on a doormat.

qa.q: What is weight?
qa.a: The force of gravity on an object
qa.e: Weight is the pull of gravity on an object, so it is a force measured in newtons.

qa.q: A school bag has a mass of 4 kg. What is its weight on Earth in newtons (use 9.8 N per kg)?
qa.e: Each kilogram is pulled with about 9.8 N, so 4 kg weighs 39.2 N.

qa.q: A box weighs 120 N on Earth. About how much does it weigh on the Moon, in newtons?
qa.e: Weight on the Moon is about one-sixth of the weight on Earth.

qa.q: Mira's mass on Earth is 42 kg. What is her mass on the Moon, in kg?
qa.e: Mass is the amount of matter in the body, and it does not change from place to place.

qa.q: Which instrument measures the weight of an object as a force?
qa.e: A spring balance stretches according to the pull of gravity on the object and reads it in newtons.

qa.q: In which direction does the Earth's gravity pull objects?
qa.e: Gravity pulls objects towards the centre of the Earth, which is why things fall 'down'.

qa.q: Why do we weigh less on the Moon than on Earth?
qa.e: The Moon pulls with about one-sixth of Earth's gravity, so weight drops. Mass is unchanged.

qa.q: Which is the correct unit for mass?
qa.e: Mass is measured in kilograms. Newton is the unit of force, including weight.

qa.q: What is the SI unit of pressure?
qa.e: Pressure is measured in pascals; 1 pascal is 1 newton of force on 1 square metre.

qa.q: A force of 300 N acts on 6 square metres. What is the pressure in pascals?
qa.e: We divide force by area to get pressure.

qa.q: The same 60 N force acts on each of these areas. Which area, in square metres, gives the GREATEST pressure?
qa.e: The smaller the area, the greater the pressure for the same force.

qa.q: Why does a school bag have wide straps?
qa.a: To spread the weight over a larger area and reduce pressure
qa.e: A larger area means less pressure, so the bag hurts less.

qa.q: Water spurts out of three holes at different heights in a bottle. Which hole sends water the farthest?
qa.e: Liquid pressure increases with depth, so the bottom hole has the greatest pressure.

qa.q: Why is a dam wall made thicker at the bottom?
qa.a: Water pressure is greatest at the bottom
qa.e: Deeper water presses harder, so the base must be strongest.

qa.q: In which direction does air exert pressure?
qa.e: Air presses on surfaces from every direction, which is why a sealed balloon stays round.

qa.q: Why do ears sometimes 'pop' when travelling up a hill road to Mussoorie?
qa.e: Higher up, outside air pressure is lower than the pressure inside the ear, until they balance with a 'pop'.

qa.q: Wind blows from:
qa.e: Air is pushed from where pressure is higher to where it is lower.

qa.q: What happens to air when it is heated?
qa.e: Warm air expands, becomes lighter and rises, letting cooler air flow in.

qa.q: During a sunny day at the seaside, the breeze usually blows:
qa.a: From the sea to the land
qa.e: By day land is hotter, air over it rises, and cooler air from the sea moves in.

qa.q: Why does the land breeze blow at night?
qa.a: Land cools faster than the sea
qa.e: At night the land is cooler, so the warmer air over the sea rises and air flows from land to sea.

qa.q: In India, the south-west monsoon mainly brings rain during:
qa.e: The south-west monsoon usually arrives in Kerala around the start of June and brings rain until about September.

qa.q: Which instrument measures wind speed?
qa.e: An anemometer's cups spin faster in stronger winds. A barometer measures air pressure.

qa.q: During a storm, a weak tin roof may lift off. Why?
qa.a: Fast wind above lowers the pressure, and the higher pressure below pushes up
qa.e: Fast-moving air has lower pressure, so the still air inside pushes the roof upward.

qa.q: What causes winds on a large scale over the Earth?
qa.a: Uneven heating of the Earth's surface
qa.e: Different places heat up differently, creating pressure differences that make air move.

qa.q: Where do cyclones form?
qa.e: Warm ocean water supplies the heat and moisture that power a cyclone.

qa.q: What is the calm centre of a cyclone called?
qa.e: The eye is a calm region of very low pressure surrounded by the strongest winds.

qa.q: The centre of a cyclone has:
qa.e: Rising warm, moist air leaves very low pressure at the centre, and winds rush in around it.

qa.q: Which organisation issues cyclone warnings in India?
qa.e: The IMD tracks storms using satellites and radar and issues warnings.

qa.q: In which sea near India do more cyclones form?
qa.e: The Bay of Bengal has more cyclones than the Arabian Sea, which is why the east coast faces them more often.

qa.q: During a thunderstorm, which is the SAFEST place to be?
qa.e: A building protects you from lightning. Tall trees, open fields and water are dangerous.

qa.q: Which item is most useful in a cyclone emergency kit?
qa.e: Power often fails in cyclones, so a torch, water, dry food, first-aid and a charged phone matter most.

qa.q: A cyclone near the Americas is usually called a:
qa.e: Hurricane is the name used near the Americas; typhoon is used in the western Pacific. A tsunami is caused by undersea earthquakes, not winds.

qa.q: Why does the smell of a burning agarbatti fill a room?
qa.a: Scent particles diffuse through the air
qa.e: Particles of the scent move about and mix with air particles, spreading through the room by diffusion.

qa.q: Sugar dissolves in a glass of water and the water level barely rises. What does this show?
qa.a: There are spaces between water particles
qa.e: Sugar particles fit into the spaces between water particles, so the volume barely changes.

qa.q: In which does diffusion happen fastest?
qa.e: Gas particles are far apart and move very fast, so they mix quickly.

qa.q: What effect does heating have on the particles of a substance?
qa.e: Heat gives particles more energy, so they move faster. The particles themselves do not grow.

qa.q: What holds the particles of a solid together?
qa.e: Particles attract each other, and this attraction is strongest in solids.

qa.q: A crystal dissolved in water colours a whole jug, and even after dilution the water stays a little coloured. What does this tell us?
qa.a: Each crystal contains a huge number of very tiny particles
qa.e: The colour spreads through a big volume because the crystal breaks into countless tiny particles.

qa.q: The spreading of particles of one substance among another on their own is called:
qa.e: Diffusion happens because particles keep moving and mixing by themselves.

qa.q: Why can we smell hot food from far away more easily than cold food?
qa.a: Hot food particles move faster and diffuse quickly
qa.e: Heat makes particles move faster, so the smell reaches us sooner.

qa.q: In which state are particles packed most closely?
qa.e: Solid particles are tightly packed with very little space between them.

qa.q: Why does milk take the shape of the glass it is poured into?
qa.a: Its particles can slide past each other
qa.e: Liquid particles can move past each other, so a liquid flows and takes the container's shape.

qa.q: Which can be compressed the most?
qa.e: Air is a gas with large spaces between particles, so pushing them closer is easy.

qa.q: Which statement about gases is correct?
qa.a: They fill the whole of any container
qa.e: Gas particles move freely in all directions and spread out to fill the container.

qa.q: The force of attraction between particles is weakest in:
qa.e: Gas particles are so far apart that the attraction between them is very weak.

qa.q: A liquid has:
qa.a: Fixed volume but no fixed shape
qa.e: A litre of water stays a litre, but it takes the shape of a bottle or a bucket.

qa.q: When ice melts into water, what changes?
qa.a: The arrangement and spacing of the same particles
qa.e: The water particles stay the same; only how they are arranged and how freely they move changes.

qa.q: Why do particles in a solid not move around freely?
qa.a: Strong attraction holds them close in fixed positions
qa.e: Strong attraction keeps solid particles in place, though they still vibrate.

qa.q: At what temperature, in °C, does pure ice melt?
qa.e: Ice melts at 0 °C. Water freezes at the same temperature.

qa.q: At what temperature, in °C, does pure water boil at sea level?
qa.e: At normal sea-level pressure, pure water boils at 100 °C.

qa.q: Why does water in a clay matka stay cool?
qa.a: Water seeps through tiny pores and evaporates, causing cooling
qa.e: Evaporation from the outer surface takes heat away from the water inside.

qa.q: Which condition makes wet clothes dry fastest?
qa.e: Heat and wind both speed up evaporation.

qa.q: Water drops on the outside of a cold glass come from:
qa.a: Water vapour in the air condensing
qa.e: Air contains water vapour, which cools on the cold glass and turns into liquid drops.

qa.q: Camphor kept open slowly disappears without turning into a liquid. This is:
qa.e: Sublimation is a solid changing directly into vapour.

qa.q: How is evaporation different from boiling?
qa.a: Evaporation happens only from the surface and below the boiling point
qa.e: Evaporation goes on at any temperature from the surface; boiling happens throughout the liquid at the boiling point.

qa.q: Why do we feel cool when sweat dries on our skin?
qa.a: Evaporating sweat takes away heat from the skin
qa.e: The escaping water particles carry energy away, cooling the body.

qa.q: What is an element?
qa.a: A pure substance made of only one kind of atom
qa.e: An element has only one kind of atom and cannot be broken down chemically into simpler substances.

qa.q: What is the chemical symbol of iron?
qa.e: Iron's symbol Fe comes from its Latin name, ferrum.

qa.q: How many elements are known today?
qa.e: Scientists have identified 118 elements so far.

qa.q: Which of these is a non-metal?
qa.e: Sulfur is a yellow, brittle non-metal that does not conduct electricity.

qa.q: Which property tells us that copper is used for electric wires?
qa.a: It is a good conductor of electricity
qa.e: Copper conducts electricity very well and can be drawn into wires (ductile).

qa.q: The symbol 'Na' stands for:
qa.e: Na comes from natrium, the Latin name for sodium. Nitrogen is N.

qa.q: Being able to be drawn into thin wires is called:
qa.e: Ductility means a metal can be drawn into wires; malleability means it can be beaten into sheets.

qa.q: Which statement about elements is correct?
qa.a: They are made of only one kind of atom
qa.e: Water is a compound and air is a mixture. Elements contain only one kind of atom.

qa.q: What is a compound?
qa.a: Two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed proportion
qa.e: In a compound the elements are chemically joined and always in the same ratio.

qa.q: Which of these is a compound?
qa.e: Water is hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined. Oxygen and gold are elements; air is a mixture.

qa.q: How many atoms in total are there in one molecule of water (H₂O)?
qa.e: A water molecule has 2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom.

qa.q: Common salt is made of sodium and chlorine. Why is it safe to eat when chlorine is poisonous?
qa.a: A compound has properties different from its elements
qa.e: When elements combine to form a compound, the new substance has completely new properties.

qa.q: How can a compound be broken down into its elements?
qa.e: Elements in a compound are chemically bonded, so physical methods cannot separate them.

qa.q: What does the formula CO₂ tell us?
qa.e: C is carbon, O is oxygen, and the small 2 belongs to oxygen.

qa.q: In a compound, the elements are always present in:
qa.e: Every sample of pure water, for example, has hydrogen and oxygen in the same ratio by mass.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a compound?
qa.e: Copper is an element. Sugar, carbon dioxide and salt are compounds.

qa.q: Which of these is a mixture?
qa.e: Air is a mixture of gases such as nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide.

qa.q: Which is a homogeneous mixture?
qa.e: Dissolved salt is spread evenly, so every part of the solution is the same.

qa.q: Brass is an alloy of:
qa.e: Brass is a mixture of copper and zinc used in utensils and taps.

qa.q: How can you get salt back from salt water?
qa.e: Dissolved salt passes through a filter, but when the water evaporates the salt is left behind.

qa.q: In a mixture, the components:
qa.e: Each substance in a mixture keeps its properties, which is why physical methods can separate them.

qa.q: Which method separates sand from water?
qa.e: Filter paper lets water pass through and holds back the sand.

qa.q: Which is a pure substance?
qa.e: Distilled water is the compound water with nothing else in it. The others are mixtures.

qa.q: Why can a magnet separate iron filings from a mixture of iron and sulfur, but not from iron sulfide?
qa.a: In the mixture iron keeps its magnetic property; in the compound it is chemically combined
qa.e: Mixtures keep the properties of their parts, while compounds have new properties.

qa.q: In a solution of salt in water, which is the solvent?
qa.e: The solvent is the substance that does the dissolving, here water.

qa.q: In sugar syrup, sugar is the:
qa.e: Sugar is the substance that dissolves, so it is the solute.

qa.q: Neha dissolves 25 g of sugar in 100 g of water. What is the mass of the solution, in grams?
qa.e: Dissolving does not destroy the sugar; its mass is added to the water's mass.

qa.q: Why is water called the universal solvent?
qa.a: It dissolves a very large number of substances
qa.e: Water dissolves more substances than most other liquids, though not all (sand and oil do not dissolve).

qa.q: Which of these is insoluble in water?
qa.e: Sand settles at the bottom however much you stir.

qa.q: A solution has the same composition throughout. So it is a:
qa.e: A solution is uniform everywhere, which makes it a homogeneous mixture.

qa.q: In soda water, the gas carbon dioxide is the:
qa.e: Carbon dioxide is dissolved in water, so it is the solute. The fizz is the gas escaping.

qa.q: Which solvent would you use to remove nail paint?
qa.e: Nail paint does not dissolve in water but dissolves in nail-polish remover, a different solvent.

qa.q: What is a saturated solution?
qa.a: One in which no more solute can dissolve at that temperature
qa.e: A saturated solution holds the maximum solute it can at that temperature.

qa.q: How can you dissolve more sugar in a saturated sugar solution?
qa.e: Raising the temperature increases the solubility of sugar.

qa.q: Why does a warm bottle of soda fizz more on opening than a cold one?
qa.a: Gases are less soluble in warm water
qa.e: Warm water cannot hold as much carbon dioxide, so more gas escapes as fizz.

qa.q: Which change makes salt dissolve faster but does NOT change its solubility?
qa.e: Stirring speeds up dissolving but the maximum amount that can dissolve stays the same.

qa.q: Solubility is the maximum amount of solute that dissolves in a fixed amount of solvent at a given:
qa.e: Solubility depends on temperature, so we must state it.

qa.q: Why can water in a very warm pond be harder for fish?
qa.a: Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen
qa.e: Oxygen is a gas, and gases are less soluble in warmer water.

qa.q: Some sugar stays at the bottom of a glass of water after a lot of stirring. The solution above it is:
qa.e: If extra solute stays undissolved after stirring, the solution has reached its limit: it is saturated.

qa.q: Which dissolves fastest in water at the same temperature?
qa.e: Powder has a much larger surface touching the water, so it dissolves faster.

qa.q: 15 g of salt is dissolved in 135 g of water. What is the concentration, as a mass percentage?
qa.e: Divide the solute's mass by the solution's mass (not the water's) and multiply by 100.

qa.q: A solution has 40 g of sugar in 200 g of solution. What is its concentration, as a mass percentage?
qa.e: The total mass of solution is already given as 200 g.

qa.q: How many grams of salt are in 300 g of a 5% salt solution?
qa.e: 5% means 5 g of solute in every 100 g of solution, so 300 g has 15 g.

qa.q: What happens to the concentration of a sugar solution when more water is added?
qa.e: The same sugar is spread through more solution, so it becomes more dilute.

qa.q: A dilute solution has:
qa.a: A small amount of solute in it
qa.e: Dilute means relatively little solute for the amount of solution.

qa.q: Glass A has 10 g of sugar in 100 g of solution. Glass B has 10 g of sugar in 200 g of solution. Which is more concentrated?
qa.e: A is 10% while B is 5%. The same sugar in less solution means higher concentration.

qa.q: 8 g of glucose is dissolved in 92 g of water. What is the mass of the solution, in grams?
qa.e: Mass of solution = mass of solute + mass of solvent = 8 + 92 = 100 g.

qa.q: Why should ORS be made exactly as the instructions say?
qa.a: The right concentration of salts and sugar is needed for it to work safely
qa.e: Too strong or too weak a solution may not help the body properly, so the concentration matters.

qa.q: The angle of incidence is 35°. What is the angle of reflection?
qa.e: By the law of reflection, the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.

qa.q: A ray makes an angle of 40° with a plane mirror's surface. What is the angle of incidence?
qa.e: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, not from the mirror surface.

qa.q: Raju stands 2 m in front of a plane mirror. How far is he from his image?
qa.e: The image is as far behind the mirror as he is in front of it.

qa.q: Why is 'AMBULANCE' written in mirror writing on ambulances?
qa.a: So it reads correctly in the rear-view mirror of the vehicle ahead
qa.e: A mirror laterally inverts the writing back to normal for the driver ahead.

qa.q: Which describes the image in a plane mirror?
qa.e: A plane mirror always gives a virtual, upright image of the same size.

qa.q: What is the normal in reflection?
qa.a: A line at 90° to the mirror at the point where the ray strikes
qa.e: The normal is a reference line at right angles to the surface, from which both angles are measured.

qa.q: A virtual image is one that:
qa.a: Cannot be obtained on a screen
qa.e: Rays only seem to come from a virtual image, so a screen cannot catch it.

qa.q: A ray of light falls on a mirror along the normal. What is the angle of reflection?
qa.e: Along the normal, the angle of incidence is 0°, so the angle of reflection is also 0° and the ray goes straight back.

qa.q: Which mirror is used as a rear-view mirror in vehicles?
qa.e: A convex mirror gives an upright image and a wide field of view of the traffic behind.

qa.q: The image formed by a convex mirror is always:
qa.e: Whatever the object's position, a convex mirror gives an erect, diminished, virtual image.

qa.q: Which mirror is used in a torch to make a strong beam of light?
qa.e: A concave reflector sends the bulb's light out as a strong, nearly parallel beam.

qa.q: A shaving mirror makes the face look bigger. It is a:
qa.e: With the face close to it, a concave mirror forms an enlarged, erect image.

qa.q: The inside of a shiny steel spoon acts as a:
qa.e: Its reflecting surface curves inward, like a cave, which is why it is called concave.

qa.q: Why are convex mirrors placed at sharp bends on hill roads?
qa.a: They show a wide area so drivers can see oncoming vehicles
qa.e: Convex mirrors give a wider view, helping drivers see around the bend.

qa.q: Which mirror can form a real image that can be caught on a screen?
qa.e: A concave mirror forms a real, inverted image of distant objects, like a window, on a screen.

qa.q: Solar cookers use concave mirrors because they:
qa.a: Concentrate sunlight onto a small area
qa.e: A concave mirror brings sunlight together to a small area, producing heat for cooking.

qa.q: A convex lens is:
qa.a: Thicker in the middle than at the edges
qa.e: A convex lens bulges outward in the middle.

qa.q: Which lens is used as a magnifying glass?
qa.e: Held close to small print, a convex lens gives an enlarged, erect image.

qa.q: The image formed by a concave lens is always:
qa.e: A concave lens spreads rays apart, so it always gives a small, upright, virtual image.

qa.q: Which lens can form an image of a distant tree on a screen?
qa.e: A convex lens converges light and can form a real, inverted image on a screen.

qa.q: The bending of light as it passes from air into glass is called:
qa.e: Refraction is the bending of light when it passes from one transparent material to another.

qa.q: A concave lens is called a diverging lens because it:
qa.e: Rays passing through a concave lens spread out.

qa.q: Why must you never look at the Sun through a lens?
qa.a: The lens can focus strong sunlight and badly damage the eyes
qa.e: A lens can concentrate sunlight enough to burn, which can seriously harm the eyes.

qa.q: Which of these uses lenses?
qa.e: A microscope uses an eyepiece lens and objective lenses. The others use reflecting surfaces.

qa.q: What causes day and night?
qa.a: The Earth's rotation on its axis
qa.e: As the Earth spins, each place turns towards the Sun (day) and away from it (night).

qa.q: About how many days does the Earth take to go once around the Sun?
qa.e: One revolution takes about 365¼ days, which is why we have leap years.

qa.q: Which of these is a leap year?
qa.e: 2028 is divisible by 4 (2028 ÷ 4 = 507), so it is a leap year.

qa.q: How many days does February have in a leap year?
qa.e: The extra day is added as 29 February.

qa.q: Around which date is the longest day of the year in India?
qa.e: The summer solstice in the northern half of the Earth falls around 21 June.

qa.q: On an equinox, day and night are:
qa.e: Equinox means 'equal night'. Around 21 March and 23 September, day and night are nearly equal.

qa.q: A gnomon is a stick whose shadow helps us track time. Why does its noon shadow change length through the year?
qa.a: The Sun's height in the noon sky changes with the seasons
qa.e: The Sun is higher at noon in summer and lower in winter, so noon shadows are shorter in summer and longer in winter.

qa.q: Why do we add a leap day roughly every four years?
qa.a: The Earth takes about 365¼ days to orbit the Sun
qa.e: Four quarter-days add up to about one whole day, which we add to keep the calendar in step with the seasons.

qa.q: Why does the Moon shine?
qa.e: The Moon has no light of its own; we see sunlight bouncing off its surface.

qa.q: About how long is one full cycle of the Moon's phases, in days?
qa.e: From one new moon to the next takes about 29.5 days.

qa.q: Which phase comes right after the new moon?
qa.e: After the new moon, a thin lit crescent appears and grows: the waxing crescent.

qa.q: Why do we see phases of the Moon?
qa.a: We see different amounts of its sunlit half as it orbits the Earth
qa.e: Half the Moon is always lit; the part of that lit half we can see changes as the Moon moves around the Earth.

qa.q: On a new-moon night (Amavasya), the Moon is:
qa.e: At new moon, the Moon's lit side faces away from us, so we cannot see it.

qa.q: The fortnight when the bright part of the Moon is growing is called:
qa.e: Shukla Paksha is the waxing (bright) fortnight; Krishna Paksha is the waning fortnight.

qa.q: On average, the Moon rises each day about:
qa.a: 50 minutes later than the day before
qa.e: Because the Moon moves along its orbit, it rises about 50 minutes later each day on average.

qa.q: A full moon is usually seen rising:
qa.e: At full moon the Moon is opposite the Sun, so it rises in the east as the Sun sets in the west.

qa.q: About how many days are there in 12 lunar months of 29.5 days each?
qa.e: Twelve lunar months add up to about 354 days.

qa.q: About how many days shorter is a 354-day lunar year than a 365-day solar year?
qa.e: 365 − 354 = 11 days, so lunar dates shift about 11 days earlier each solar year.

qa.q: Which calendar adds an extra month now and then to stay in step with the seasons?
qa.e: Lunisolar calendars add an extra month (Adhik Maas) about every two and a half to three years.

qa.q: The Gregorian calendar is a:
qa.e: It follows the Earth's revolution around the Sun, with leap years to match about 365¼ days.

qa.q: In which year was the Saka calendar adopted as India's national calendar?
qa.e: India adopted the Saka calendar as its national calendar in 1957.

qa.q: The first month of the Indian national (Saka) calendar is:
qa.e: Chaitra is the first month and usually begins on 22 March.

qa.q: Why do festivals fixed by a lunar or lunisolar calendar fall on different Gregorian dates each year?
qa.a: Lunar months do not fit exactly into the solar calendar
qa.e: Lunar months (about 29.5 days) do not line up with Gregorian months, so the dates move.

qa.q: The extra month in a lunisolar calendar is called:
qa.e: Adhik Maas means 'extra month'; it is added so festivals stay in their seasons.

qa.q: What is an ecosystem?
qa.a: Living things interacting with each other and with their non-living surroundings
qa.e: An ecosystem includes both living and non-living parts and how they interact.

qa.q: Which is an abiotic (non-living) part of a pond ecosystem?
qa.e: Water is non-living; fish, algae and ducks are living.

qa.q: Which of these is a biotic (living) part of a forest?
qa.e: Fungi are living decomposers. Sunlight, air and rocks are non-living.

qa.q: The Sundarbans is famous for which type of ecosystem?
qa.e: The Sundarbans in the Ganga-Brahmaputra delta has the largest mangrove forest in the world.

qa.q: Can a single rotting log be called an ecosystem?
qa.a: Yes, it has living things like fungi and insects interacting with moisture, air and wood
qa.e: Ecosystems can be small. A log has its own community of organisms and non-living conditions.

qa.q: Why can a camel survive well in the Thar Desert?
qa.a: It is adapted to hot, dry conditions
qa.e: Camels can go long periods without drinking and have features suited to heat and sand.

qa.q: Which is NOT an ecosystem?
qa.a: A plastic bottle kept empty on a shelf
qa.e: An empty bottle has no community of living things interacting, so it is not an ecosystem.

qa.q: Which pair shows a living thing and a non-living factor that it needs?
qa.e: A plant (living) needs sunlight (non-living) to make food. The other pairs are both non-living.

qa.q: In a food chain, the producer is usually a:
qa.e: Green plants make their own food from sunlight, so they start food chains.

qa.q: In the chain grass → rabbit → fox, the rabbit is a:
qa.e: The rabbit eats plants (grass), so it is a herbivore, or primary consumer.

qa.q: In a food chain, the arrow points from:
qa.e: Arrows show the direction in which food and energy move: towards the eater.

qa.q: What is the original source of energy for almost all food chains?
qa.e: Plants capture sunlight in photosynthesis; this energy then passes along the chain.

qa.q: Which of these is an omnivore?
qa.e: A bear eats both plants (fruits, honey) and animals (insects, fish).

qa.q: What do decomposers like bacteria and fungi do?
qa.a: Break down dead remains and return nutrients to the soil
qa.e: Decomposers recycle nutrients from dead plants and animals so producers can use them again.

qa.q: A field's grass holds 10,000 units of energy. Roughly how many units reach the grasshoppers that eat it (about 10%)?
qa.e: Most energy is used or lost as heat at each level, so only about a tenth moves up.

qa.q: Many food chains linked together in an ecosystem make a:
qa.e: Animals usually eat more than one kind of food, so food chains join up into a web.

qa.q: What is interdependence in an ecosystem?
qa.a: Living things depending on each other
qa.e: Organisms rely on each other for food, shelter, pollination and more.

qa.q: How do bees help plants?
qa.e: Bees carry pollen from flower to flower, helping plants form fruits and seeds.

qa.q: If all frogs vanished from a paddy field, what is most likely to happen?
qa.e: Frogs eat insects, so without frogs, insect numbers would rise.

qa.q: In the same field, what would likely happen to the snakes that eat frogs?
qa.e: With less food available, the snake population would likely fall.

qa.q: Which shows plants and animals depending on each other for gases?
qa.a: Plants release oxygen; animals breathe out carbon dioxide
qa.e: Animals use oxygen from plants; plants use carbon dioxide in photosynthesis.

qa.q: A bird eats a jamun and drops the seed far away, where a new tree grows. This is:
qa.e: Animals spreading seeds to new places is seed dispersal.

qa.q: Which human activity most upsets the balance of a forest ecosystem?
qa.a: Cutting down large areas of trees
qa.e: Deforestation destroys homes and food of many organisms at once.

qa.q: Why are vultures important in an ecosystem?
qa.e: Vultures feed on carcasses, cleaning up the environment and helping prevent the spread of disease.

qa.q: About what percentage of Earth's surface is covered by water?
qa.e: About 71% of the surface is water; the remaining 29% is land.

qa.q: Why can liquid water exist on Earth's surface?
qa.a: Earth is at a suitable distance from the Sun
qa.e: Earth's distance from the Sun keeps temperatures in the range where water stays liquid.

qa.q: What does the ozone layer do?
qa.a: Absorbs most of the Sun's harmful UV rays
qa.e: Ozone high in the atmosphere absorbs most ultraviolet radiation that can harm living things.

qa.q: Earth's position from the Sun is:
qa.e: The order is Mercury, Venus, Earth, so Earth is the third planet.

qa.q: About what percentage of Earth's water is salty sea water?
qa.e: About 97% of Earth's water is in the salty oceans, so fresh water is precious.

qa.q: Why is Earth not too cold, even at night?
qa.a: Its atmosphere traps some of the Sun's heat
qa.e: Gases in the atmosphere act like a blanket that keeps some heat in. This keeps the average temperature around 15 °C.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a reason why life is possible on Earth?
qa.e: Earth has no rings. Water, oxygen and a suitable temperature all support life.

qa.q: Most of Earth's fresh water is:
qa.a: Frozen in ice caps and glaciers
qa.e: Most fresh water is locked up as ice, so the water in rivers, lakes and underground is a small, precious part.

qa.q: Which gas makes up the largest part of air?
qa.e: Nitrogen is about 78% of air, much more than oxygen (about 21%).

qa.q: About what percentage of air is oxygen?
qa.e: Oxygen makes up about 21% of air.

qa.q: How many litres of nitrogen are there in about 200 litres of air (78% nitrogen)?
qa.e: 78% of 200 litres is 156 litres.

qa.q: Which chemicals damaged the ozone layer?
qa.e: CFCs, once used in old fridges and aerosol sprays, break down ozone high in the atmosphere.

qa.q: In which year was the Montreal Protocol to protect the ozone layer signed?
qa.e: The Montreal Protocol, signed in 1987, phased out ozone-damaging chemicals.

qa.q: What is the natural greenhouse effect?
qa.a: Some gases in the atmosphere trap heat and keep Earth warm
qa.e: Gases like carbon dioxide trap some heat, keeping Earth warm enough for life.

qa.q: Why is too much carbon dioxide in the air a problem?
qa.a: It traps extra heat and warms Earth more
qa.e: Extra greenhouse gases trap more heat, leading to global warming and climate change.

qa.q: Which gas do plants take from the air to make food?
qa.e: Plants use carbon dioxide, water and sunlight in photosynthesis.

qa.q: What does biodiversity mean?
qa.a: The variety of living things in an area
qa.e: Biodiversity covers all the different plants, animals and microbes of a place.

qa.q: In which year was Project Tiger launched in India?
qa.e: Project Tiger began in 1973 to protect tigers and their habitats in tiger reserves.

qa.q: Using old glass jars to store dal is an example of:
qa.e: Using something again for the same or a new purpose without remaking it is reuse.

qa.q: In the Chipko movement, villagers protected trees by:
qa.a: Hugging them to stop them from being cut
qa.e: 'Chipko' means 'to cling'. People hugged trees so that they would not be cut down.

qa.q: A school saves 4 litres of water a day by fixing a leaking tap. How many litres does it save in 30 days?
qa.e: Small savings every day add up: 4 × 30 = 120 litres.

qa.q: Why is burning garbage harmful?
qa.a: It releases smoke and harmful gases that pollute the air
qa.e: Burning waste, especially plastic, releases harmful smoke that damages health and the environment.

qa.q: Which is a protected area for wildlife in India?
qa.e: National parks, wildlife sanctuaries and biosphere reserves protect plants and animals in their natural homes.

qa.q: Which action best reduces air pollution from transport?
qa.a: Using public transport, cycling or walking for short trips
qa.e: Fewer vehicles on the road means less smoke and fewer greenhouse gases.
